And if we could go to page 2 in the English -- page 3 in the English version, under -- page 2 in the B/C/S. Under item 2 you will see that -- we will see from -- the third paragraph we'll start. It says: "HDZ must remain totally mobile. It is the only political power of the Croatian people which is capable of confronting Greater Serbian policies." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So -- by that we mean -- when we're talking about Greater Serbian policies, we're also talking about the war that is being waged or that is about to be waged by the Greater Serbian policies; right? Or as a result of these particular policies; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It refers to the aggression against Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the next -- very next line, it says: "There is a possibility that the conflict may spread from Croatia to the territories of BH." So as early as 4 April, 1991, the alarm bell is being sounded off, that there is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the next point is: "That the people -- Croatian people remain peaceful and dignified but it is also necessary to know how to physically protect the people if the need arises. This is expected from us, and it is our duty to do so." So again, HDZ, taking it upon itself to be the political power of the Croatian people, is very mindful of its responsibility and the necessity of the Croatian people to at least self-organise themselves. At least, that's how I interpret it. Would that be correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was our duty given the situation and the electoral results.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And then the very next one, it's -- it says: "The standpoint of HDZ towards the army is clear. The army must defend the external borders and must not become involved in inter-ethnic relations." Now, when we're talking about the army, which army are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The official army, the Yugoslav People's Army. It was called that way but already at the time it was in fact absolutely Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And for all intents and purposes, if we step back, in the former Yugoslavia, the JNA was for the entire country, which was made up of several republics and some autonomous regions, and now the JNA for all intents and purposes has become the Serbian army and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina does not have an army other than the Territorial Defences which, as you noted, at some point are stripped of all of its weapon stockpiles; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The only army on our soil was the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Now, if we go to the -- the second to last paragraph on page 3 in the English version, it talks about the need for 24-hour presence at the offices of the HDZ Municipal Boards. It's still on the second page. It says: "This is going to be a very long and difficult month in the terms of the political situation and Municipal Boards are asked to remain mobile and to ensure 24-hour presence ..." And this by and large is because of the situation that is unfolding; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we, as we sit here today in this courtroom, can only imagine -- can only imagine the situation, how it was back then, but for you and your colleagues and the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, particularly those who were on the fringes of where the fighting was going on, for them it was a very surreal situation, one which they had not experienced before but one that certainly was very troublesome, to say the least.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I don't believe there's anything other -- anything else in this -- let me go on. There's one more in item 3, just very briefly. It says here on item 3 -- it's one, two, three -- the fourth paragraph. I'll read it. It's on page 4 of the English version, page 3 for you. It says: "In some municipalities, because of the build-up of internal party problems, it is necessary to carry out preparations for extraordinary HDZ assemblies in order that higher quality personnel are elected to the leadership of the party." In my conversation earlier with you where I said that there was -- there are some difficulties at this particular time because everybody's learning how to work within a democratic process, the party is rather new, the circumstances are incredibly difficult, expounding the situation, and here is a situation where you say they need to exercise more care in finding and ordering higher-quality personnel; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're saying now is only part of the problem. The other part of the problem was that for the elections many serious-minded people, well educated, did not wish to accept the HDZ. But later on, with the development of events and the introduction of the -- or, rather, the advent of the danger from a Serb aggression, they came to understand they must stand by their people. And then we took in many more serious minded, educated and so on citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But that took a while. That took some time.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we gave them an official status. That's why we set up these extraordinary assemblies in the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And then on a very -- just the very last page, on page 5 for us, right -- slightly above your signature line, you'll see your name. It says: "Stjepan Kljuic will always -- will always invite one of the vice-presidents to be present at inner party negotiations." It's page 3 for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's -- and I'll read the English version and then, as I understand it, Your Honour, it's been -- perhaps the gentleman can read it in B/C/S and it can be translated, because as I understand it, it's -- there's a mistake, and I apologise for self-correcting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, if you could read that for the record, because -- so we can have an accurate translation.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always had at inter-party negotiations to take one of the deputy presidents and a member who would be an expert on the subjects under discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, but if you could read it, just for the record, what it says. Because the English version is slightly -- there might be a mistake in the English version, just so we could have a correct translation. If you can just read it where it says: "Stjepan Kljuic ..."

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At the inter-party negotiations, Stjepan Kljuic always called somebody some vice-president."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's it. Okay.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the vice-presidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, these inter-party -- just to make sure that we understand, these inter-party negotiations, what are you speaking about?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period when we won the elections and when the new government was established, we had to replace the entire state apparatus, and the easiest thing to do was in parliament, because the situation was clear there, as it was indeed in the Presidency, and when we came to set up a government, too, where all the nations were represent. However, you must understand that that was still -- it was still a communist country that we were living in and where everything was state owned. Perhaps because the former Prime Minister, Markovic, there might have been 3 to 5 per cent of private ownership in the business world, but as these companies and enterprises were very important politically, economically, and socially speaking, they had to be taken over, and those places had to be filled. On the other hand, what we needed to do was to replace, in the federal representative offices in Belgrade and in the sphere of diplomacy, the old cadres, and that was a slow, painstaking process especially because of the system of voting that was in place. Some people had terms of office from the previous elections for the Federal Assembly, for instance. And generally speaking, the process was a slow one and an unwieldy one, and there was resistance in having the new powers that be take over all these functions. That's why we set up these commissions, we invited people to attend sessions we organised. We even invited people who didn't have to be necessarily a member of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just -- so as I understand it, depending on the availability of positions that had to be replaced or filled, the parties, among themselves, would make proposals as to -- they would work out the numbers to make sure that their -- that every ethnic -- every nation had its number of people at every level; correct? You're shaking your head. Does that mean yes?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only in the top echelons of the state did you have parity, whereas in the other parts it was proportionate representation. And we had some formulas, 5, 4, 3, 4, 2, et cetera, these ratios, 4, 3, 2, 3, 2, 1, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the party itself, for instance the HDZ in this instance, it would try to locate and designate the appropriate Croats to fill those -- those seats that were available to the Croat nation, the Croat people; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we'll get to it in a little bit, but that was a long, painstaking process, trying to find, identify the right people, making sure that they had a background clearance, they weren't Communist oriented or had been part of the last Communist system, had the qualifications. No? Okay.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but you know, you couldn't find somebody who hadn't been a Communist. And we had a principle of reconciliation, so we just didn't take the extremist Communists who had done evil to the Croat people and other people within the police force, for example. But if a professor of economics had been a Communist before, that was tolerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. As long as he wasn't an extremist. And as I understand, that took up a lot of your time, your personal time, this process.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did, but we had a cadres commission of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if you would like me to explain this to you, I can do so briefly. We tried --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to get to it. I just wanted to touch on that. And we're going to get to it, though, because as I understand, that was one of the major issues within the party, one of the criticisms that was lodged against you or the leadership, that they weren't acting fast enough to fill in these positions, and there was a sense of frustration. I'm not saying that those accusations were necessarily true or not, but nonetheless they existed there; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was true, but it was very difficult to find the right people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Right.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suitable people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree. I totally sympathise with you. Now, if we can get to 00034, the next document, excerpt of minutes dated 16 April, 1991. If we look at item 2, going back to our -- our chapter of predicting the conflict, on item 2.1, it states: "Due to further --" page 2 for you but it's under item 2.1: "Due to the further deterioration of the political situation in the homeland, round-the-clock duty must be continued in the municipal boards and BH HDZ secretariat to ensure timely dissemination of information." So here once again the alarm is being rung for 24-hour vigilance. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we have a technical problem, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's going to take a few moments to put right, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we'll stick with that document, incidentally, just so -- while this -- okay. We'll go to item 3. I don't know if the -- okay. Relax, everyone. It's under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may inquire, sir, do you have it on your screen? Good.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I have now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we could go to page 4. And under item 3, just very quickly, it says: "The members of the Presidency were informed of the political and security situation in the homeland." And then it says: "The situation is judged to be extremely serious, and HDZ members are called on to be sensible and do nothing on their own initiative in a political context without specific instructions from the HDZ headquarters. Any rash or tactless move could have unforeseeable political consequences." Now, here it appears that you're trying to warn the members to be very careful because the situation is extremely precarious; correct? Not just politically but also militarily.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then you go on to say: "At the moment, the worst hot-spots in Bosnia-Herzegovina are in the Bosnian Krajina and Eastern Herzegovina. We condemn any attempts to change the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina." So here the HDZ is condemning any changes to the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And -- and then you go on to say: "We must do everything to calm the Croatian population in the areas at risk and to ensure their peace and safety." Right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It would appear, would it not, sir, that as -- at this period of time it's becoming eminently clear that the Croats are going to self-manage, if I can use that term, self-manage in making sure that they have the necessary wherewithal to protect themselves. One, to be vigilant and, two, to perhaps arm themselves -- organise themselves and arm themselves for the eventuality of an outbreak of war; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The problem was how to protect all the Croats, not just a part of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly, because you had areas where -- that were predominantly Croat, other areas where the Croats were fewer in numbers, in a minority. And of course Bosnia-Herzegovina, depending on the area, too, that you had particular hot-spots; right? And so that was one of the problems. And the only existing formula, if I could put that, or the only thing that was at least familiar to the folks back then was this Territorial Defence concept where, at the municipal level, the municipalities would sort of ensure that they had the arms to protect the municipality itself, not outside the municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then, of course, that poses a problem. That poses a problem, because, you see, if a municipality is only looking after itself and maybe the neighbouring municipality also might be at risk, maybe down the road but not necessarily at risk at that particular point in time, may not necessarily come to the aid of its neighbour because, again, each municipality is looking after its own well-being, hence the reason or hence why the municipalities may need to pull themselves together, to pull themselves together so as they have -- collectively they may be able to assist each other in time of need.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put forward two theses here. One is a hypothesis that there were weapons, and you're talking about the other one when the weapons had already been confiscated. As you were able to see from the previous documents, we insisted that the party municipal bodies link up for easier subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's forget about the weapons, whether they had them or not. The concept that I'm proposing is based on the model that was -- that was known to the folks. One, each municipality would take care of itself, based on the concept of Territorial Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a concept that could not apply, because if everyone had been armed, one municipality could not go to another. It was only when there were weapons that those who received weapons from the JNA could go against the other municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but just work with me. We're going to go step-by-step. Under the territorial concept -- Territorial Defence concept, the municipalities were to look after themselves, not after other municipalities; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so if one municipality came under attack, they could not necessarily rely on other municipalities coming to their aid under the concept as it existed back then; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not certain, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Needless to say, the Croats at least realised that their safety lied in numbers and lied in the collective grouping of municipalities in order to self-protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And out of that concept -- out of that concept we have the HVO, which was in essence nothing more than a bunch of Territorial Defences, municipalities organising themselves, pooling their resources together so that they, collectively, would be able to protect not just their own municipality but protect others?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to object at this point, Your Honour. For one thing, the evidence is pretty clear that Mr. Kljuic was not involved at the time that the HVO was formed in April of 1992. He was no longer in the party or involved in those efforts at all. If counsel can establish some personal knowledge of this witness to talk about the HVO, we could possibly do that. But again, beyond that, my second basis of objection is again the characterisation by Mr. Karnavas for facts that are not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond. The gentleman was a product of the former Yugoslavia. He -- he was a member of the Crisis Staff. As you told us, everybody was forming Crisis Staffs, including HDZ. He obviously -- everybody was taught about civil protection, including the Territorial Defence. It was thought in the high schools, if I'm not mistaken. Everybody was mobilised. I mean, this country was highly, highly prepared in the eventuality of a war, because the JNA was not an army for offensive purposes but merely for defensive purposes. And the whole concept of the All People's Defence was that, along with the JNA, you would have -- at the municipal level you would have the Territorial Defence working side by side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if I'm mistaken, sir, perhaps you can correct me on all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In order to enable the Judges to understand this question properly, Witness, did you do your military service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I did. I was a reserve captain. I went through officers' school in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you went to the officers' school in Bihac [as interpreted] and you were a reserve captain. So if we were to understand the term "Territorial Defence" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I graduated with the rank of 2nd lieutenant, and then every year I went for further training and I arrived at lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Captain, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were a lieutenant, so defence is something which means something, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You listened to the question that was put to you by Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Karnavas was putting forward a theory. He was saying that, given the fact that there was no army, that there was a Territorial Defence, that the municipalities had to unite in order to counter a potential attack, this idea which was put forward by Mr. Karnavas, in other words the creation of the HVO, is a theory which you agree with or disagree with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Please. When the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina was at its fiercest, the people organised in whichever way they could. We had three components. One was the HVO. The second was another smaller Croatian association, the HOS, the Croatian defence forces, and the third was the Territorial Defence. We in the Presidency were happy for anyone to stand in defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but there was not a single command. So we tried to create a framework for all these three components, and we adopted a decision that they should all be part of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In this way, all this was legalised. However, problems later occurred between the HOS and the HVO. As for the Territorial Defence, it was to grow into the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Just one point I would like to clarify. You just talked about the HOS. What does the HOS stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is an old Croatian political party, and in the Republic of Croatia where the aggression began before it did in Bosnia-Herzegovina, this party created a volunteer organisation to defend the state. Its name was the Croatian Liberation Forces; HOS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one -- just to go back a little bit. As I understand it, after serving -- after one served his military service, they were in essence in the reserve up until the age of 60 or 65 under the old system; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact -- and in fact, the municipalities had a well-established Territorial Defence office, and in the eventuality of a mobilisation, either for military purposes or for natural disasters, everybody knew, the women and the men, knew exactly what they needed to do. Enterprises knew how they would need to contribute. Is that correct? In other words, it was very well structured.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could go to the next document, and that would be P -- D -- no, P 00041. Just very briefly. We're going through this rather quickly. Again, item 1 on this document. This is excerpts from the minutes of the HDZ BH Presidency. The date is 10 July, 1991. So now we've moved on a couple of months down the road. On the agenda, item 1. It's at the bottom the page in English. It says: "The situation in the entire homeland was estimated as extremely dramatic and that due to aggressive Greater Serbia policy, a widespread armed conflict may be expected at any time." So here we see that the situation seems to have gotten worse. More predictions of war. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we were to go to the end of the -- end of this document, we would see that it was signed by you. You were one of the signatories. So in essence you were part of this particular meeting where again the issue of a widespread conflict looming in the air was being discussed. If we could go on to the next document, and that would be P 00042, generated on 21 July, 1991. This is a Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina Travnik region meeting at Busovaca. We can see from the top paragraph that you were present. No, I'm sorry. It says on the basis of the conclusion, I apologise, and based on the decision of HDZ BiH president Stjepan Kljuic, there's a meeting here. And if we could go to the conclusions. In English it would be on page 2. And it would be page 2 for you as well. Under paragraph 2 -- well, paragraph 1, it says: "Croatia is in a state of war." By that we're talking about the Republic of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then we -- then in number 2, it says, and this is rather interesting: "A silent occupation is being carried out in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the same invader."

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And so at this point in time -- at this point in time, 21 July, 1991, the silent occupier is none other than the JNA, and they're on territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and as we discussed yesterday, they're using Bosnia-Herzegovina as a launching pad to attack the Republic of Croatia. Right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army was still the regular armed force, because Bosnia-Herzegovina was part of Yugoslavia. So was Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, that's what -- and -- and -- it would be fair to say that it's a rather confusing period of time. I mean, the very same army that's -- the very same army that's supposed to be protecting you is now launching attacks against a neighbour; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency of Yugoslavia, which was supposed to stop that army, was unable to do so. And you will see that it says the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina couldn't stop the army. Well, it couldn't. You can't use the hands of a civilian to stop a tank. The JNA was conquering particular territories within Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you will later see that this was all in accordance with the Ram plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I intervene to correct a probable error? You have said, Mr. Kljuic, the Presidency of Yugoslavia was unable to stop the attack, and you would probably -- you wanted to say the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. At that time, the Presidency of Yugoslavia was in existence. Jovic, Drnovsek, Mesic, Tupurkovski, Bogicevic, and others were in it. We had the same level -- the same system at state level and republican level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was hoping --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So why, according to you, did the Presidency of Yugoslavia not want to stop the JNA in its tracks? Because usually an army is dependent upon the government of the country.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In every democratic country the army obeys the civilian government. However, in Yugoslavia you had people advocating Milosevic's policies and democrats fighting against them. But Kadijevic and Adzic, they were the minister of defence who didn't obey the Prime Minister, and the commander-in-chief of the armed forces did not respect the intervention of the Presidency. This means that the army was out of the control of the civilian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for having clarified this, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Karnavas, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I was expecting you to correct me when I said that Bosnia-Herzegovina was used as a launching pad to attack a neighbour, a neighbouring state, in other words, because obviously Croatia at that time was still a republic within Yugoslavia. Just -- correct? I mean, this is what's happening.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not until later when you have -- it declared its independence, then we can speak about the JNA using Bosnia to attack another country, but in this particular period it is used -- Bosnia-Herzegovina as a republic, the land is used there as a launching pad to attack another republic within -- within Yugoslavia. And that was -- that was part of the problem at the time.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The republic of -- not the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was not the official policy of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Simply a part of the territory which was occupied by the JNA on the Bosnian-Herzegovinian side was being used as a launching pad to fire on Croatia. But the same was happening within the Republic of Croatia. The JNA and the Chetniks had conquered certain areas so that from Mirkovac they were firing on Osijek. And when they told me, "Why don't you stop them using Nova Gradiska in Bosnia as a launching pad to shoot on Croatia?" And I said to them, "Well, why don't you stop them doing that from Mirkovci?" You have to understand that the legal authorities at the time, both in the Republic of Croatia and in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina were unable to stop the JNA. In Croatia at that time, there was already a police and an army, but we didn't have that in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just -- I guess we should just stick with this a little bit to make sure that we're clear. By -- in this period in history it's clear that Yugoslavia is breaking up, one way or another.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was quite clear, but it hadn't happened yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It hadn't happened yet. And now you have the army, the JNA, and as we said, it was there for self-protection, not for offensive purposes, it was there to protect against invaders. Now the very same army that is there to protect is being used to attack certain republics within -- within Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we could say that this is a civil war going on. That's one way of putting it. But because of the make-up of Bosnia -- of Yugoslavia, we know --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Hold on. Let me finish my question, please. When I pose a question, then you can answer it. You have within Yugoslavia various republics, some of which -- some of which aspire to have -- to be independent; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it was not a civil war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no, please, sir. If you could answer my question. Were there not several republics within Yugoslavia that aspired to be independent from Yugoslavia? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Withdraw your question about the civil war and I will answer you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I withdraw that question. This is the question that's being posed to you.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent. Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So now that we are in agreement. Now, one of those republics at some point in time was going to have to make a decision, that is Bosnia-Herzegovina, whether it was going to stay within the former Yugoslavia or the Yugoslavia as it existed back then, or whether it would take a path, as Slovenia did and as Croatia was doing, and become independent. Obviously they were going to have to make a choice at some point - they, it - Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And while this you have this -- this play going on between JNA in Slovenia, JNA in Croatia, Bosnian territory is being used by the JNA in attacking another republic; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a game in Slovenia, but in Croatia there was aggression. But, yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I guess that's why we had that conversation yesterday, because I wanted to make clear, and I thought we had reached an understanding at the end of the day but maybe we hadn't, that some Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina felt an unease with Izetbegovic after he made the proclamation, "This is not our war," because, after all, they were on the front line and the JNA was using Bosnian territory to attack Croatians, and so that was part of the mix of the atmosphere at the time, part of the confusion.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now that we got that cleared, going back to this particular document, document P 0042. We talked about the silent occupation. That was on point 2. If we could go to point -- if we could go to point 4. Here it says that President Kljuic is ordered to call an urgent session. I'm told I need to go above one line, to paragraph 3, so let's do that first. "The Croatian Democratic Union has declared a state of emergency and is demanding the HDZ BiH Presidency to take a stand on this and initiate adequate measures." I guess that's what I was talking about a little bit earlier. The BiH Presidency to take a stand. Right now it's on the fence. They're waiting to see who is going to win. Is it going to be Serbia with the JNA or is it going to be Croatia? And they want a clear message from the Presidency, as a collective body of which Izetbegovic was the president, they want a clear stand: Where does BiH stand in this situation given that there's a silent occupation? Isn't that a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, you're wrong on two counts. You keep mixing up the Presidency of the HDZ and the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the HDZ, we adopted a conclusion that we should take a stand and take certain measures. These measures were subordination, sending information about movements of the JNA, and - why not say it? - collecting weapons --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- while the activity of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina was on another level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. All right. Let's move on to -- to -- if you go to -- we'll skip -- we'll fast forward to item 12, which may be on the next page, page 3 for you. It says here: "The BH government has done nothing about resolving the new situation in a satisfactory manner." When we're talking about BH government, we know who they're talking about, do we not? Those are the folks in Sarajevo. I understand you made the distinction you're not part of the government, you're part of Presidency which sits on top of the government, but it's pretty clear, is it not, that there is dissatisfaction with what is happening at the state level. And I'm not suggesting that they could have done something, but I'm just -- I just want to be clear on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Far be it from me to try to help Mr. Karnavas be more efficient, but I just wonder, haven't we talked about these things about five or six times now in the last several hours, and what's the point of asking about what the government didn't do when Mr. Karnavas has said repeatedly he admits they had no ability to do anything. So why do we keep doing it over and over and over again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I can explain that, Your Honour. I can explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We have document after document after document, and that's what I'm doing; I'm showing progressively, they're asking do something, do something, do something. Now we have a silent occupation mentioned for the first time. We're talking about a state of emergency. And if we're going to look at the events in context, one of -- when it goes to the joint criminal enterprise, the Prosecution would have us believe that the self-protection of the Croatian people is a joint criminal enterprise. That's why. And so now we're hearing it and we're going to see it progressively that the government is impotent, is unable to do anything. Not only that -- not only that, but he admits to the president of the Presidency sending mixed messages. And one of the messages is, "If you're Croat, don't expect any help from us." That's what the message is. And that's -- that goes to the joint criminal enterprise at least in part. So why the Croatian felt it necessary to organise themselves at the grassroot level, why the HVO was organised. And then we're going to see so on and so forth later on why it's necessary, even at the administrative level, to organise. Hence, no joint criminal enterprise; self-protection, self-preservation, self-determination. That's what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott has just remarked, Mr. Karnavas, on the fact that you asked the same questions yesterday and you're asking the same questions today. We understand fully that the question is part and parcel of what you wish to demonstrate, but please try to avoid asking the question several times over. Mr. Scott, you are still on your feet. What would you like to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honour. I just note most of the documents -- almost -- virtually all of the documents that Mr. Karnavas has used in his cross-examination are documents that have been admitted as part of the Prosecution case. You have all those documents. We put those documents in. The Judges can read all these points. None ever this was kept from the Chamber. It's all in the documents the Prosecution put into the record, and again I just don't know that we have to say the same things five or six or seven times. As to -- as to the question that, Did at some point Bosnian Croats take efforts to organise themselves? Yes, they did. I don't think there's any dispute about that whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will do so, Your Honour. I will do so, and I will endeavour to be non-repetitive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Getting back to the same document, sir, I'm going to move -- I'm going to skip some parts since we lost a little bit of time and go to item 6. You will see at some point -- I don't want to read the whole thing, but at some point it says: "The relations with the other parties ..." And then afterwards, it says, "A clear stand if the SDA decides to remain within the Rump Yugoslavia or, rather, Serboslavia; about the statement made by the president of BiH Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, that he requires the representatives of BiH to attend a conference of Islamic countries, even without previous consent of the Presidency; and other topics ..." Now, from item 6, I didn't read the whole thing, but obviously they want a clear position, are they not? This is what is being asked.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, some people at that time were impatient. They would set an ultimatum. Either for us or against us, they would say. But I wasn't like that. And it was very important to hold Izetbegovic and the SDA from going over to the SDS -- going over to the SDS and JNA side. Now, as far as the departure of the delegation to Jeddah for the Islamic conference there, that was the desire for Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a state populated by Muslims, to become an observer in that international organisation, and Bosnia-Herzegovina to that present day is an observer, although I don't see any great benefits to be reaped from that. But anyway, at the time they probably wanted to ask for assistance for the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which they did indeed receive later on, but I prayed to God they never received that aid and assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But I guess, getting back to the point, and I understand that folks might have been impatient out in the field, out in the areas where they were close to the front line rather than being in Sarajevo, which ultimately later on comes under siege, but here they're asking for the SDA, which is the Muslim party, to make a decision. They want a clear -- they want a clear answer. Where does Izetbegovic stand in his party, because as you noted, the Serbs, they're looking for a partner, and they want to know, is Izetbegovic with us or is he with them, them being the ones that are doing the attacking. And I think that's a legitimate question, don't you? One that needed to be answered at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. That was the key question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We couldn't put an ultimatum to anybody, but it was a very good thing that Izetbegovic didn't join the SDS, didn't go to that side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand. And I've never met the man, but he was an associate of yours, and some say, as you rightly pointed out here in the Balkans, some of us have -- say one thing in the morning and do something else -- or decide to do something else in the afternoon. Izetbegovic was a man that was very ambivalent at times, and it was very hard to get a clear, stable, unmovable answer from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that a speech or a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's a question based on his experience of having worked with the man who is no longer here to be sitting in the dock.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course I cooperated, and that's how it emerged that Mr. Izetbegovic did not cross over to the Serb side. We were partners, not colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't ask you whether you were --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want you to bring me into a situation where you would refer to me as being a colleague with Karadzic. We were partners. So not colleagues; partners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Izetbegovic, was he not known of not having taken a very firm and clear stance, one which troubled the Croats at the time, which is why they're asking for the SDA, of which he was the president of - and he was also the president of the Presidency - to take a clear stance? Isn't that a fact? If you can answer my --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how it was: The fact is that Izetbegovic did not cross over to the Serb side and that the Bosniak Muslims did not cross over to the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a fact. And that a large number of them defended Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. What part of the question did you not understand, you being a very intelligent human being. I'm asking you about Izetbegovic as a politician, because these are troubled times and people in the field, people that you were supposed to be responsible for were asking for a clear message. Is it not a fact, sir, that during that period of time Izetbegovic, being the politician that he was, never gave a clear and concise answer in that period of time as to where he, the SDA, the Muslim nation, stood? And this is in light of the comments that he made, "This is not our war," after a Croatian village gets massacred. Is it not a fact that he never gave a clear answer and now they're asking him to. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't judge by the speech, the speeches made by Izetbegovic. You have to judge him on the basis of his conduct and behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could answer my question. Why would the Croats be asking for a clear stance of the SDA if they had one? Is it not a fact that Izetbegovic was not giving a clear answer because he wanted to have it both ways. And he was negotiating with the Croats, he's negotiating with the Serbs, he's sitting on the fence. He's waiting to see where the winds blow, who wins, and then he's going to make his decision. I'm not saying it's good or bad, but that's the way it was; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, if you ask the witness to say what the intention of Mr. Izetbegovic was, is that not inviting him to speculate? I remember having heard such objections from the Defence side addressed to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, normally, under some circumstances that would be an excellent objection. Under these circumstances, I would say in light that the gentleman worked closely with the -- and we can look at circumstantial evidence, that -- hence the lengthy question, because I'm giving him enough there, facts one can judge. But my -- I'm asking a very simple question. Did he give a clear stance to the Croats? Yes or no. Where does he stand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, there's a question that you were asked, and you were asked to answer yes or no, give a yes or no answer. That is to say whether Mr. Izetbegovic had a clear-cut position with respect to that issue and problem. So you can say he didn't have a position, his position was very clear, I don't know, or whatever. So that's what we want to hear, without speculation, of course. Because you were working in the Presidency. So we would like to know what you thought about the situation which was described in the document, in paragraph 6, in fact. And that document wasn't signed by you, it was signed by Dario Kordic, but since at the time you were the president of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you must have had a point of view. So what was your point of view? Did you have one or not? And when we hear that answer, the Defence can continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. If a regional organisation of one particular party sets an ultimatum to the president of the other party, then the president of that party is not duty-bound to respond to the question at all. And it is my life-long trouble and problem to see that Izetbegovic didn't cross over to the Serb side, because he wasn't clear on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt here. You were asked a very specific question. Now, if the gentleman doesn't wish to answer the question maybe he can just tell us that he doesn't wish to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I will answer the question, but just explain to me what duties Izetbegovic had towards Kordic to answer the question he was asked in that way. Just explain that to me. How? Reading it in the papers?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, let me go back. Did Izetbegovic -- forget about Kordic. I'm asking you. Did Izetbegovic at that point in time take a firm stance, give a clear stance on what the SDA, that represented the Muslim nation, planned, keeping in mind -- keeping in mind that he's the president of the Presidency and he does - I dare disagree with you - but he does have an obligation to respond to the folks, the people, the citizens that live within Bosnia-Herzegovina, given his position. So did he have a clear -- did he have a clear stance? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what his stance was, but he acted in a satisfactory manner at that stage. And as far as I was concerned as president of the HDZ, that was very important, that he didn't join Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on, Mr. President, and I apologise for wasting time on this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to number 11, Kordic, along with the others that attended, say: "The Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina with their vague and generalised declarations did not contribute to resolving the political situation created in BiH and Yugoslavia." Would you agree or disagree with that? That would be a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At those meetings an agreement was never reached. Not because of Bosnia-Herzegovina but because all the participants disagreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking about -- the statement here is that, "The Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina --" of which you were a member -- "with their vague and generalised declarations -" empty words, in other words - 'did not contribute to resolving the political situation created in BiH." Do you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How about number 12? Do you disagree with: "The BiH government has done nothing about resolving the new situation in a satisfactory manner." Agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, when you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you agree or disagree with that, sir? Because we have to move on. You can either agree or --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why -- listen here. I have my position, you have your position. Perhaps you're in a hurry; I'm not in a hurry. I'll come back for another five days, if need be, but I don't want to give hasty answers nor do I want to say something that was not my stand. There is a gradation here, and that means in our language that probably the government did what it could but not what it should have done perhaps, or what we wanted it to do perhaps. The fact remains that it did not do better and could not have done better than it could have done. I'm not defending the government, but that's the situation, what the situation was like. You must be aware of the fact that this is written by a man in a small place and now you're discussing global issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. As opposed to a big man in a big place, such as yourself in Sarajevo. But that --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Oh, come on. No. But you have to be aware of the fact and know that in a chaotic situation of that kind the person with more information knows more. So it's easy to put the question in the form of an ultimatum when you have no obligation of receiving an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we did -- if we go to 14, it says: "The Ministry of National Defence is impassively watching the mobilisation of the reservists in BiH being carried out without its consent." Agree or disagree with that? This is the Ministry of National Defence. This would be at the Yugoslav level.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the ministry didn't have any weapons and the reservists, under force of arms, were mobilised. Croats and Muslim Bosniaks fled whereas the Serbs went voluntarily, of their own free will. They couldn't wait to join up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Number 16: "The BiH economy is in a state of total collapse and social unrest of large proportions is in sight. The present authorities are powerless in their attempts to consolidate -- to -- to consolidate the situation." Would you agree or disagree that at that point in time in BiH the economy was virtually in a state of total collapse? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And -- and I would take it that that would cause some concerns of the folks out -- you know, the little folks out in the various areas, regions.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they first of all did what they could to save their lives and then their property. Heads first, property second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And one would expect that there's a -- if the economy is in a state of total collapse, that municipalities might have to fend for themselves, and might have to sort of organise and perhaps even join with other municipalities to sort of try to see how they could best weather out the storm?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then it says on 17: "On the basis of all these conclusions we urge the Croatian population in the Travnik region and Herzegovina municipalities to join the Croatian -- the Croatian Regional Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina." So I assume, based on your previous answer, you would agree that this is a good conclusion.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a position on that, but it's a good thing for them to associate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And at some point we see that they're also calling for a Croatian National Council to be formed because others have already formed their national councils. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. By the way, I just want to make sure that, you know, you talked about Izetbegovic and -- and -- I mean, politicians do what they have to do in very difficult times. They're entitled to be ambivalent, and they're entitled to hold several conflicting positions at the same time. Is it a fact or not that at the time -- at that period of time Izetbegovic was also being courted -- being courted by the Serbs, just as the Croats at some point were?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very intensively so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And hence your earlier answer, which I agree with, hence why it was very important on your part, on your part, to make sure that he didn't cross over to the other side. Right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I succeeded in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We'll give you credit for it. And so while this young upstart politician in a rural area is sort of impatient and pushing you, you on the other hand, being in the eye of the storm, having perhaps more information, you're trying do everything you can, perhaps not as quickly or to the satisfaction of others, and that, as I understand it, was part of also the misunderstanding within the party. They thought you weren't moving fast enough and thought you were at least politically in bed with Izetbegovic. You had become his puppet. Isn't that a fact? That's what they thought. I'm not suggesting that it was true.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they can think what they like, but that's not true. It was only thanks to me and some other people that Izetbegovic didn't cross over to the other side, and that's a very important point, because the aggression against the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina would have started a year earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And I take it you -- you being in Sarajevo and having access to information also knew that -- I guess it was around August 2, 1991, of the agreement with the Serbs between Filipovic and Zulfikarpasic. That's one of those names I just can't pronounce. Zulfikarpasic. Right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's even more difficult for you to understand the situation. First, they didn't reach an agreement with the Muslims because the main Muslim party, the SDA, in parliament, in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, had 86 deputies. When Milosevic and Cosic, through the cultural circles, did not succeed in attracting the Muslims, Milosevic opened variant B, went to plan B and called upon the other Muslim party, the Muslim Bosniak organisation, which had only two deputies, two representatives in parliament out of 240 seats. This attempt to make a historical agreement with Zulfikarpasic was an attempt finally to liquidate the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because had the agreement been reached, and it provided for the fact that between the JNA forces, the Serb population, and the Muslims, there would not be a military conflict but that all outstanding issues would be resolved through agreement, given a situation of that kind, it would mean that only the Croats would be the destructors and destroyers of Yugoslavia. They would be the secessionists, and along with Belgrade propaganda, which always characterised us as Ustashas and a genocidal nation. I know how I contributed to toppling that historical agreement. I don't want to go into that now, but it was a major political success, the fact that the Muslim people did not accept Zulfikarpasic but remained loyal to the SDA party, the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Now, this was not such a secretive event that nobody knew about it. In other words, word was getting out that the Serbs were courting the Muslims and the Muslims were trying to cut deals with the Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, lots of things were recounted, but luckily for me, an agreement was not reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, but just hear me out again. At that time -- at that time, while this was happening, this information was also known to others. It wasn't just known to you. The point that I'm trying to make is when folks out in the region are hearing that this is the sort of thing that's happening, that Izetbegovic and his -- and his colleagues are being courted, and perhaps even proposing to enter into agreements, those are the sort of news -- that's the sort of news that one hears and becomes alarmed. Not knowing, of course, that, thank God, you were on the scene to make sure that it didn't happen. But nonetheless the folks in the region are becoming increasingly alarmed at that sort of news, hence even more of a reason for folks in the regional level to organise themselves for the eventuality of a war.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's quite normal, but don't bring me into a situation where I challenge the right to self-organisation, arming, and so on. That's something that I advocated. I'm not disputing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You advocated that. That was one of the things that you had advocated.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. What ought I to have done? To leave the people unarmed? It's quite another matter that I as a politician didn't have access to the resources, money or weapons, but other people did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And incidentally -- okay. Just to make sure that it's very clear, that agreement, the historic agreement between Filipovic and Zulfikarpasic, that was also recounted in the press at the time so that God and mankind would have known about it, not just you.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they learnt a little later, learnt about it in general terms, but the details were accessible to just a narrow circle of people. But the image of the talks and negotiations was negative for the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And perhaps a question that might be -- that might be in everyone's mind, when you said that if they had made the agreement, war against the Croats would have started a year before. Could you tell us -- explain that a little bit to us. What do you mean by that? The significance of it.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's very simple: Had the Muslims accepted cooperation with the Serbs -- and on that level a number of meetings were held at different levels. For example, on one occasion Dobrica Cosic, a leading Serb man of letters, writer, on behalf of the Serbian national elite invited Muslim intellectuals to come to Belgrade. Then on another occasion Milosevic invited Izetbegovic secretly and offered him the post of president of the Yugoslav Assembly. Not to speak of Karadzic, Krajisnik, Koljevic, who permanently asked for opposite numbers among the Muslims. And when that didn't succeed, they went through Zulfikarpasic. But that doesn't succeed either. Had it succeeded, then the Yugoslav People's Army, which had weapons, which had a command staff, would have mobilised 300.000 Muslims and with the necessary propaganda would have sent them into Croatian territory, and you can assume what would have happened then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we can move on really quickly because we have a few moments before the break. I just want to cover the rest of this. If we could move to the next document, 00047. This is dated 6th of August, 1991. Main Board of the BH HDZ. Just very quickly. If we could look at number 4. On your page it would be page 3. This is item 4. It says here: "The Main Board of BH HDZ states the fact that the Croatian people are in a state of war and that it and its territories are subjected to direct occupation by Serbia, which is helped by a part of the JNA and other paramilitary Chetnik units." Again, one more alarming sign.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you go to paragraph 5: "The government of BiH is requested to prevent the 14th Corps of the so-called JNA from coming to BH, Bosnia-Herzegovina." Of course, wishful thinking at the time, given that the government of BH is unable to do anything, but nonetheless it's there; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that it was unable. They didn't ask us. There was already a military dictatorship at the time on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Then it goes on to say further down, the very last one on page 5, I don't know what -- it should be still page 3 of yours: "If the BH government ignores these resolutions, we shall demand that it be called to account or possibly to resign." Threatening, fighting words I see coming out of the board, Main Board of the HDZ, which, incidentally, bears your signature at the end. So you, too, now, like the young upstart from the woods, is also calling for the BH government to account for itself and to resign if it fails or ignores these particular resolutions, albeit you know in your heart-of-hearts at that particular time they're really incapable of complying with many of these resolutions because of the circumstances on the ground.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is your description of those people, not mine. That's one thing. Another thing: Of course we exerted pressure on the government, and even made threats that they should resign, but we would never have allowed them to resign, because that's what the Serbs wanted, and even greater chaos would ensue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So as a politician, being the politician that you were, and politics is a life of compromises, you put your signature on a document knowing very well that a resolution such as this one in actuality is meaningless, but nonetheless you go along with the crowd, if not leading them.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was leading them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Exactly. Then if we could just go to 16 -- paragraph number 16. It's on your page -- it's on page 5 on your page, the B/C/S. It says here: "It is considered that the war is gradually being transferred to Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that the HDZ leadership must be constantly alert. In order to try to normalise the situation and avoid causing panic in the field, it is considered that there is still no need for the BH HDZ to introduce state of emergency in the party." That was your sentiment at the time. But then you go on to say: "If there is a direct -- if there is a direct danger of war in an area, the Municipal Board, after consultation with the leadership, will introduce a state of emergency." And this, of course, is 6 August, 1991. So we've moved from April, and we've found ourselves in August.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could go to the next document, and that would be P 00052, dated 26 August, 1991. It comes from the BH HDZ Presidency, excerpts of the minutes. We can see on page 1 that you attended the meeting. And we can look at the agenda later on. But if we could just go through the -- if we could go to the conclusions, conclusions reached. On number 10. I think we'll just do this one. The rest, as the Prosecutor indicated, we can read on our own and draw our respective conclusions. "The BH HDZ Presidency requested that the BH government and its organ urgently convene a meeting of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina which must take a position on the status of Bosnia-Herzegovina in light of recent events and on the stationing of fascist military units in Bosnia-Herzegovina which has become a staging ground for the aggression against the Republic of Croatia." Sounds to me, Mr. Kljuic, that you're now sounding a little bit like Mr. Kordic. You, too, leading this meeting, are also saying that something has to be done. You're asking the BH government and its organs to urgently convene a meeting, and you're asking for a position on the status of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I take it by August 26, 1991, you're saying the very same thing that we talked about back at a meeting that was chaired by Mr. Kordic; correct? A few months earlier.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't compare us. It's inappropriate. Not because I'm trying to make out I'm an important person, but we are not on an equal footing. As you can see I and the leadership of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina was seeking a legal route. We were seeking an Assembly session, and we wanted to get the Serb delegates, or at least a majority vote, to condemn the fact that the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina was being used as a launching pad for firing on Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. If we look at number 7, it says here: "President Stjepan Kljuic should attend the next meeting of the Travnik BH HDZ regional organisation in order to resolve all misunderstandings that have arisen to date." Now, the misunderstandings that they're talking about, could they be that at this point in time they don't know where you, the president of the HDZ, stands on this position because they perceive, rightly or wrongly, they perceive you not to be pushing Izetbegovic, not to be pushing the SDA, not to be pushing the BH government in taking a clear stance in light of all what is happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina? It's near midnight and nothing is happening. Might that be the misunderstandings that they're talking about?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Please. Every party has its misunderstandings. Take any leader. I'll be modest and I won't draw comparisons with other parties, but there are always people who disagree among themselves. Of course it was my wish to smooth this out and regulate it. In any case, we were trying to work through the institutions of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina to improve a situation that was not good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we go back to 10, it says: "The BH Assembly must also take a position on the silent and perfidious occupation of the BH aggressor." So they're not asking not just the government but the Assembly. Incidentally, where does the Assembly sit in comparison with the government? The government is the executive. Is the Assembly below or above? And perhaps you could also tell us where the Presidency sits.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly is above, but you have to know how an Assembly session is called. There is a collegium of the Assembly composed of representatives of all the parties, and to call an Assembly session you need 40 deputies to sign unless it's a regular session, which is called by the Assembly leadership. We tasked our deputies with initiating an Assembly session, and then we would take the floor and ask the Assembly to take a stand on the aggression against the Republic of Croatia, the arrival of the army, and the abuse of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just to finish with this document, because we have to go to lunch. Perhaps you could give us a short answer. May I ask why you as a member of the Presidency didn't also -- and you were attending - in fact chairing - this meeting, why didn't you ask the Presidency of which you were a member to also take a position? I mean, perhaps it wasn't -- it wasn't easy to order the government to take a position. It wasn't easy to order the Assembly to take a position or convene, let alone take a position, but why not just ask the Presidency, since you were already on the Presidency? Why not ask the very same body and put it in here? Any particular reason, or that escaped you at the time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency asked more than once the Presidency of Yugoslavia to put the army under the control of the civilian bodies, because we in the Presidency were not competent. We wanted to, but we didn't have the power to give orders to the army. The Presidency constantly did this but without any result.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But my question was this: Why didn't you also, you know, put yourself into it? You know, a little self-criticism. It was kind -- I know the bygone days of communism and socialism where self-criticism was somewhat in mode, but at this point in time why not say, "You know what? We should ask also from the Presidency to take a clear stance." Since you were on the Presidency. And then you could say, "Well, the HDZ has requested, where do we stand, guys? Where do we stand as a Presidency so at least we can communicate this to the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina because we're trying to make sure that we don't split apart, that we don't have these ethnic, you know, differences?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kindly answer this question, please. It was a question I was going to put to you myself yesterday. Could you answer this question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We often raised this issue and submitted it to the higher instance in Belgrade. As for self-criticism, don't ask me to do that. That was a Communist virtue. Unfortunately, I was not a member of the League of Communists. They would not accept me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question wasn't answered. We could break for lunch and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we shall have a break for an hour and a half and resume close to 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.34 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are now resuming our hearing. Just one point I'd like to clarify. Before we -- we broke up, I said I wanted to ask the same question as the Defence team had. I'm only talking about content. I'm not talking about form. That said, I give the floor back to Mr. Karnavas. We have another hour and a half before we have our next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And the Defence always welcomes questions from the -- from the Bench for clarification, and we hope that we are assisting the Bench with our questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Kljuic, if we could go back so I can close this chapter, I just have two -- two minor documents to show you. One is dated on the 26th of August, 1991. It's P 00051. If you can just look at it. We're still on -- unfortunately, on the second chapter -- the third chapter, predicting the conflict. This one, we see this is a statement that is being issued, a public statement, is it not? Condemning the use of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a staging ground. Right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then in the last paragraph it states: "In expectation of war, we might -- In expectation of war which might soon spread to Bosnia-Herzegovina ..." and then it goes on urging, once again, the JNA to think of the historical, that they will be held accountable. But more or less, again, the expectation that war is about to spread to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Finally, if we could pull up P 00060, dated 8 October -- 8 October, 1991. And I would -- that would be on page 2 of your -- your document, sir. If we could look at paragraph number 5, under "Conclusions." And again, see as we started in April, now we're in October, and here on page -- on paragraph number 5, "The decision of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina about the neutrality of Bosnia and Herzegovina is -- is endorsed, but --" it comes with a big "but." "... but with a condition that Bosnia and Herzegovina may not and will not be a military training ground for continued aggression." Just touching on that, we did speak about it yesterday. For all intents and purposes, Bosnia and Herzegovina was a military training ground or launching pad, I would say, by this point, since we've been talking about the events since April. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At least here by this point, October -- October 8, 1991, we finally -- at least we could conclude that some sort of a -- a public statement, some sort of a decision, some sort of an announcement was made by the Presidency of Bosnia, of which you were a member of about the neutrality of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So finally there is that which was asked by Kordic and then eventually by you. Finally we have something here tangible, albeit not much more than just rhetoric.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we can move on to the next area, and -- let me have a moment here. Sticking with the topic, basically, or somewhat connected to what we were speaking about, loss of weapons. That's what we're going to call this particular chapter. I just want to bring to your attention P 00058. If we could just discuss this for a second. It's a document dated 18 September, 1991, HDZ, Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and if we could look at that. We'll look at point 1 here.
