The Security Council is now called the Crisis Staff. It takes on a different name. This was the same Security Council that we spoke about earlier which you were the chairman of, as I believe, or you were appointed to; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 3 under -- under point 1, it says: "The Crisis Staff shall start working immediately and shall be in charge of the entire system of the defence of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina to ensure the acquisition of weapons." You see that? It's the third paragraph --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. It's the third -- it's the third --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see point 1 at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well -- it's the -- hold on. Hold on. I'm going to direct you. Relax. No need to get excited. Page 1. You told us you were a calm man. Page 1.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only told you that it's not on my screen. I didn't say anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is it on your screen now, sir? If not, I have a hard copy for you.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, if we look at point 1, I just read that out, where the Security Council is now the Crisis Staff. Now, if you look at the third paragraph under point 1, it says here: "The Crisis Staff shall start working immediately and shall be in charge of the entire system of the defence of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and ensure the acquisition of weapons." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we were to go all the way to the end of the -- of the document, of course, we would see that you have signed this as president of the HDZ. Now, I take it, sir, given that you were a member of the Security Council which then became the Crisis Staff, you immediately embarked on an enterprise to acquire weapons in order to protect the Croatian people, at least at the local level. Did you do that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the president of that Crisis Staff, and it was not possible for me on my own, or anyone on their own, to protect the Croatian people. As for obtaining weapons, I said yesterday that we were in contact with the Republic of Croatia, and in view of the position of certain regions where this was possible, we tasked two members, two vice-presidents; Mate Boban and Iko Stanic. One of them was assigned to Western Herzegovina and the other one to Posavina to carry out the technical part of the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. The technical part of the job, that is making sure that -- that -- that weapons are acquired for the protection of the Croatian peoples. We're speaking now September 1891 [sic] -- 18 September, 1991; right? So this was tasked to them by the Crisis Staff of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we recall, earlier today we went through one of the documents where -- it's on the record, where it indicated that the HDZ undertook the obligation or saw itself as the one in charge of the protection of the rights of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we were to continue on to the next page, it would be page 2 on my document, and I believe it might be page 2 on yours as well, it says here, and I'll read at the top of the page, first paragraph on page 2 in English: "In case of an armed conflict on a territory with a predominantly Croatian population, the Crisis Staff shall take over all government functions in the municipalities, and the work of the BH HDZ shall be suspended until the threat of war is over; i.e., until it is deemed to be over by the Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But here it is expressly said, "in case of." So it's not an order that comes into force on the same day but which will be issued later if it becomes justified. In case this happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree with you. That's -- you know, I just want to make sure that this was something, a document generated by the HDZ Security Council with you heading it, chairing it, and where you task others, including Boban, and here you foresee the possibility that -- that should a conflict come into place where Croats are the predominant nation, the Crisis Staff takes over all governmental functions in the municipality. And I take it what you mean by that is administrative functions; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is not something unusual, by the way, this sort of -- of a precautionary measure. This was something that was ingrained going back again to the Territorial Defence, because as I understand it, and of course I didn't grow up with it for 50 years where the people were trained and drilled on it, but as I understand it, in the eventuality, for instance, a municipality was overrun by the enemy, it would reconstitute itself someplace else and from there it would -- it would operate. Not just militarily but administratively. In other words, it would -- it would move out of danger, and wherever it could, take care of the --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such instances, but what was basic was defence on the ground. It's little satisfaction if somebody drives you off your own ground and you set up an administrative representative office far from your home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that. But I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I -- may I ask for a clarification? When one speaks of Crisis Staff here, is it the central Crisis Staff of which you have spoken first page of this document, or is it a municipal Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This was the central party Crisis Staff. But for you to understand the context, at that time the state had its own Crisis Staff, the Presidency did, the government did, all the parties did, every municipality did. So we did too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Including the municipalities. The municipalities had --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The municipalities had Crisis Staffs. Isn't that correct? So even at the local level.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Every municipality that could had a Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And so -- and then within the HDZ, just to make sure I understand it, and I might be wrong, but along with this Crisis Staff, and this ties in with the questions from Judge Trechsel, aside from this Crisis Staff at the central HDZ, if we want to call it that, there were -- you would have municipal Crisis Staffs within the HDZ. So -- and they would all be linked up. And I believe we saw some documents earlier to that effect.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I think -- let me -- if I could go to number 4, just very quickly. It says: "It is the duty of the person representing the BH HDZ in government bodies to continue performing the task conscientiously, bearing in mind primarily the interest of the Croatian people."

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, it's very important for you to understand this. The setting up of our Crisis Staffs was not incompatible with the participation of our officials in the state apparatus. We continued working in the state administration, but we were focusing on the interests of our people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, first of all I want to thank you very much for that clarification. That was the point that I was trying to establish. Obviously I missed it. I'm glad you picked it up and I hope we all understood that, that establishing the Crisis Staff under those circumstances was not only necessary but it was legitimate and proper and, most importantly, it was something that had been ingrained in the philosophy of the All People's Defence, which was the military doctrine that existed in Yugoslavia with the JNA on the one hand, the territorial on the other, protecting the motherland against invasions; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, getting back to number 4. And incidentally, this is very important for all of us to understand, because we didn't live through that area -- that -- that period. To show that it is not an anomaly, in other words. It is not something that one side or the other side did. Everybody was responsible. And since we have three nations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, every nation then took it upon themselves to ensure that they were protected even though they occupied a geographical space called Bosnia-Herzegovina. Am I correct on that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Crisis Staff had a different task, to help organise people in case of an emergency or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. And it was not just militarily, for military purposes. It was for natural disasters and other events; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And personal tragedies, personal disasters too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And while I'm on the topic, in the spring of 1991, we see, just as the Croats were trying to organise themselves and to arm themselves, we see the Muslims doing the same thing with the establishment of the Patriotic League; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now, whether it was the Patriotic League or not that is questionable, but that they organised themselves, that is true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And -- well -- and only if you know, sir, only if you know: It's my understanding that the Patriotic League, in fact, got a start on the Croats. In fact, they had begun to organise themselves, and they had established themselves before -- before the Croats. Am I correct on that or could I be off? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody can know that, because they were illegal moves so that, apart from the Patriotic League, the Bosniak Muslims still had some berets of some kind. I can't say exactly. Nobody can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you say berries, you mean they were tucked away for a rainy day? Is that what we're talking about? Oh, berets, I'm sorry. I got it wrong. I apologise. So going back to paragraph number 4, it says here: "Stjepan Kljuic shall contact the leadership of the SDA without delay and ask them to state their policy, but the Crisis Staff shall develop an action plan with or without the SDA and take specific steps with this direction." This is now September, 1991 - 18 September - and so you're now asked again, it seems -- this is through the Security Council of the HDZ, of which you were chairing, so in other words you as the chairman of the Security Council were tasking yourself or had been tasked by your colleagues to contact the leadership of the SDA presumably because you resided in -- in Sarajevo, as did the leadership of the SDA, and find out what their policy was and were they going to be with the Croats or against the Croats. Am I right on that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that it was a very difficult time and that we wanted at all events that the Bosniak Muslims be with us, because in that way all the defence tasks would have been easier to accomplish. However, even if we were to agree upon that in principle, in the field it was different to implement it. On the other hand, there were municipalities where people, without asking us in Sarajevo, achieved agreements of that kind. So we wanted to make a front with the Muslims, a defence front, and that is why we keep saying what their position and stance was. However, since we're dealing with preparations, you have to take all the options into account, and then we made a programme for if the Muslims were with us, but we had to have a second variant if we were left on our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I guess from that I can conclude that, since you're being asked to inquire and since you are also making alternative plans, a second variant, at that particular point in time in history, that is 18 September, 1991, in spite of all the other attempts, you still don't know where the SDA stands, even though presumably you would be having day-to-day contact with Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in principle we did know, because for as long as they supported the actions that we did, they were with us, regardless of whether they had gone public with it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But of course as we -- as we talked about earlier, in a not so public way they were also having contacts with -- with the enemy, the perceived enemy, and there was always that lurking danger that they would be cutting a deal behind the Croatian back, hence the reason why again it looks like as late as 18 September, 1991, clarification is requested with you directly making contact to make sure to find out what exactly are their plans; who are they with. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, the state of Yugoslavia was still in existence. The State of Bosnia-Herzegovina was still in existence. Parliamentary meetings are held. Presidency meetings are held. Government meetings are held. The Muslims did not agree to a historical agreement. Now, the fact that a peripheral Muslim party attempted to reach an agreement or contract with Milosevic was not effective. On the other hand, if you see from point 7 here -- as you can see from point 7, we're preparing stocks, military locations, and doing everything hypothetically, although not even in that year of 1991, during the first -- nor the first three months of the following year were there any conflicts that would be exclusively directed against the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The SDA wasn't a peripheral party. It was the party for the Muslims; right? I mean, it's not some fringe that they have, you know --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MBO was a peripheral party. MBO. That was peripheral. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it discussed the issues with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm trying to say is here you're being asked -- the SDA, without delay, to ask them to state their policy. They're asking you, the SDA. Izetbegovic, was he not the president of the SDA at that point in time, as well as the president of the Presidency? So it would appear that you're being tasked as chairman of the Security Council, which was -- became the Crisis Staff as of that moment, to make inquiries, to find out. So we're not talking about --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did make inquiries. I made inquiries every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And incidentally, I was just reminded. Recently it was indicated that -- on television I believe it was Mr. Filipovic who went on television and said that Izetbegovic had sent him to meet with Milosevic to cut a deal. Were you aware of that, Mr. Filipovic's acknowledgement of that on television? You being in Sarajevo, and I assume he's in your neck of the woods.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally didn't hear about that, but it might be true and here's why: Izetbegovic did not accept direct talks with Milosevic, but probably he knew that Zulfikarpasic was going, as was Filipovic, and we knew this when this was published. I can only assume that Izetbegovic thought in the following way: If the Muslim nation agreed to that option, he would too. That was his line of thinking. However, this was not by chance. But we were not still either. And anyway, the Muslim nation did not agree to the historical agreement. So that ultimately when Izetbegovic saw that his people did not lend their support to that, he distanced himself from it. And let me also mention as far as those negotiations are concerned, this: You must remember that there was the state of Yugoslavia, the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that meetings were being held every day, of parliament, of the government, of various commissions, and that all of us were located in two buildings in Sarajevo. We ran into each other every day. We talked to each other every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But Milosevic wasn't in Sarajevo. He was in Belgrade. Okay.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I described that case to you. The two men that I mentioned left, they returned, they didn't get the SDA's support.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. And another take of that story would be, or Izetbegovic's position, is a term that was used during the Watergate period in the United States with respect to President Nixon, it gave him what they called "plausible deniability." I'm not having any contact with the Serbs. I'm not having any contact with Mr. Milosevic. Now, if somebody else is, I don't know. Maybe. It also gives him that plausible deniability, sending his agents while at the same time saying I'm not meeting with him. We could look at it that way, could we not, as well? I'm not suggesting that that was the case, but there's two ways of looking at this. The coin has two faces, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I'm just going to have to say, Your Honour, we continue to have speeches that are just speeches, and there's a difference -- I know on cross-examination you can ask leading questions. I'm fully familiar with that. There's a difference between a leading question and a speech followed by nothing more than even a yes or sometimes there's almost no response at all and it's the next speech. I'm going to object this afternoon to that. I'm just going to say right now that I'm going to object to it all afternoon, if necessary, and also speculation by this witness about this theory of deniability.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, avoid speeches and get to the heart of the matter, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you one final question on this. Do you know whether those agents or representatives of Mr. Izetbegovic went there with Izetbegovic's knowledge and acquiescence and instructions or were they sort of self-managing on their own? It calls for a yes or no. If you don't know, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, only Izetbegovic can know that, and he has died.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he never disclosed anything to you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not receiving the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he disclosed that nothing had come of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which would presume that he knew they were going to meet with Izetbegovic, that they were there with his acquiescence.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe they did have that agreement, acquiescence. Why not go to Belgrade? But when everything was put on the table, what Milosevic offered, the Muslims did not accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I guess what I'm trying to also establish is others, perhaps, within the Croatian Community and within the Croatian leadership, may not have been able to understand the nuances of this game as you would have. They might have perceived, perhaps, that Izetbegovic and the SDA, representing the Muslim nation, perhaps are not to be trusted and that's why we need some clear guidance as to where they stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So again, Your Honour, is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It is a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't see a question mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There is an inflection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, you must know that everyone sought to save his own skin. Secondly, everybody talked to everybody else. But the result is the vital point, and up to that time Izetbegovic did not cross over to the Serb side. And with further developments, we were to see when he would do that. You'll learn of that in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Before we leave this document, if we could go all the way to page 5 just so we can understand the structure. I want you to look at it and tell me whether this is correct. On the last page it has a diagram. It says diagram, and then it says "Structure of regional Crisis Staff," where it says commander, assistant, liaison officer, information officer, security officer, logistics, quartermaster, medical corps, Municipal Crisis Staff -- and I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Karnavas. I wanted to step in because I've just seen that in the document there was a schematic, but we haven't got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honour. I don't have the schematic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you want to use it, perhaps we could place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we -- the schematic is actually just a list. We can put it on the ELMO, but it's the -- it would be on page 5 of the document. If you don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We have no page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We have no page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I totally apologise. If we could put it on the ELMO. We have an extra copy. It's P 00058.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine now. We can see it on our screens. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So this was the -- the structure of the regional Crisis Staff that was decided by the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we can see, answering His Honour's question, Municipal Crisis Staff, same structure as regional, so we know this was a template to be used at a municipal level as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we could move on to -- to another document, and this is 1D 00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Before we move over -- on to the next document, I have the following questions: Can we go back to page 1 of this document now, please. Mr. Registrar, can we have page one back. The B/C/S document. And paragraph 1 contains a list of the members of the Crisis Staff. It begins with your own name, Witness, then there's Mate Boban, et cetera. And I can see in last place there's Bruno Stojic. Can you tell me, please, what he was doing there in that Crisis Staff. What position was he within the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a member of the Crisis Staff, and that was on the grounds of his working in the police. As you can see, we have the Defence Minister here, Jerko Doko, as a government member, and all the officials like Branko Kvesic, who is the second assistant in the police force. Thanks to the ministries they worked in -- or, rather, they were members of the Crisis Staff according to the ministries they worked in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The members of that Crisis Staff of the HDZ, were they there because they belonged to your political party, or were they also there by virtue of their function, post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can see that in line 1 we have the president and vice-president. Then we have members of the government, the ministries -- ministers and deputy ministers - Bozo Skravan is the deputy minister for telecommunications - and then you have people from the ground, probably presidents of regions. They were Zeljko Raguz for Stolac, Dario Kordic from Busovaca, Ivo Lozancic from Zepce, and Mijo Tokic from Tomislavgrad. And some of the members, on the basis of something else, were from other places. Such as Mate Boban. He was from Grude. And Jerko Doko was from Mostar. Filip Evic was from Samac. So you had the president, the vice-president, the minister, deputy ministers, and representatives of the individual regions represented there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what about Mr. Stojic? He was there because he had a post in the police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He and Branko Kvesic were our cadres within the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Second question that has nothing to do with Mr. Stojic is this: With respect to the procurement of weapons, the Crisis Staff decided to procure weapons. Now, in order to do that, you need money, money to procure weapons. So how did you do that? Did you have a budget? How was this financed? Or did you expect to get weapons by donations or things like that? Could you tell us how you were able to equip men with weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this was very simple, you see. From the pre-election campaign in 1990, many people gave money donations to the Croatian Democratic Community, most of this money coming from expat Croats working from Australia, America, and so on. Most contributions came from our workers in Germany, for instance. And they were most numerous from Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, all the money accrued went to Zagreb, to the treasury there that was in Gunduliceva Street, and they took all our money. Then we had to ask them for weapons in return. So it was very rarely that any of us from Bosnia-Herzegovina, for instance, individually procured weapons by purchasing them from individuals or anything like that, because you must know that at the time there was a fair amount of trade in weapons going on. Serb officers stole from the JNA and sold weapons to the Muslims and Croats, for example. So there was a dynamic trade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm sure we'll come to that, but I saw Counsel Nozica on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes. I wanted to clarify something, but I'll do that when my turn comes. Thank you anyway, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I want to go to another document, that was 1D 00524, and so we're going to be stepping back a few months. The previous document was 18 September, 1991, and we're going to go to a document dated 24 and 26 of June, 1991, which might also assist the Trial Chamber, particularly in light of the questions that were raised. This document, do you have it on the screen, sir? Oh, sorry. We have an extra one for -- in English. If we could just put the English one on the -- on the ELMO. First let me just ask some questions about what the document is. From the title of the page, it says Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Would it be correct to say that as of June 24th and 26th, 1991, Bosnia was referred to or was officially known as the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- and it's -- the title says "Minutes of the meeting of the 18th session of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, held 24 and 26 of June 1991." Sir, during that period you were a member of the Presidency. Do you by any chance -- can you confirm that indeed this session took place as it's stated on what purports to be an official document, albeit an unofficial translation for the Trial Chamber and for the rest of us.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And does the document look familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it looks familiar but there's nothing there to jog my memory 15 years on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could look at the next page, under minutes of the meeting. Perhaps if we go down memory lane it might help you a little bit. We're not going through all of the minutes, just the relevant minutes. It says here that the session had been presided by president of the Presidency of Alija Izetbegovic of the -- you know, the SRBiH, Alija Izetbegovic. He indeed was the president of the Presidency, was he not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So we see your name there, Stjepan Kljuic, along with Biljana Plavsic and the others. So at this time we can also probably conclude that the Serbs of Bosnia-Herzegovina are still participating in the -- in the government, in -- in the affairs of the Republic of --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And of course we see other names. And then we get to the agenda. But let's skip over the agenda and look at item 3. And for the record, that would be -- you'll see a number on the page, 00931718. I'll read it in English and hopefully you will find it. It says here: "The Presidency has analysed the information of the Republic headquarter of Territorial Defence of BiH on the current situation of arms and the ammunition in public companies, the Opinion of the Council of General National Defence on this matter and the measures which are prescribed by the Government of SRBiH for keeping of weapons left in the companies." It goes on to say: "It was determined that there are no safety and technical conditions for keeping of weapons in the firms and that it is necessary that it would be transferred to a safer place." Next paragraph: "It was stated that the actual political-safety situation was inconvenient for the redrawing -- for redrawing the weapons for keeping them in the JNA facilities, where the weapons of Territorial Defence were kept -" past tense - "but even further consequences would have non-principal decision by which all the companies would not have the same position." Finally, it states: "The Presidency has concluded that the drawn weapons, before transferring to the JNA warehouse, would be first offered to the Ministry of Internal Affairs of SRBiH for its needs in accordance to adopted formative organisation." Now, first of all I want to make sure that more or less that is what is stated in the official version or the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is correct except that you read incorrectly something in the second passage. At least, that was the translation I received, that the situation was favourable for the withdrawing of weapons, whereas it says that it was unfavourable for the withdrawal of weapons to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. With that clarification, let's talk about this a little bit. This is June, 1991. We've gone through the document dated 18 September, 1991, where the HDZ Security Council, to be known as the Crisis Staff, is now urging the Crisis Staff, or the Security Council, to go out and acquire weapons. Here in this particular document a few months earlier, the government -- or the Presidency - the Presidency - has made a determination that whatever weapons are with public companies to be, in essence - in essence - given to the JNA, but before that, first -- just hold on and listen to the question before you shake your head -- first MUP, the Ministry of Interior is to see the weapons to see what if any of those weapons they want before they're being turned over. Is that the essence -- and we'll discuss this in detail, but is that the essence of the decision that was taken at the 18th session of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to go step-by-step, sir. Just trust me.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're starting from the wrong premises and you're incorrectly quoting the text. Please read the second paragraph again and then we can agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I'll -- if I go down to the third paragraph, which relates to my question, it says: "The Presidency has concluded that the drawn weapons, before transferring to them -- before transferring to the JNA warehouse, would be first offered to the Ministry of Internal Affairs of SRBiH for its needs in accordance to adopted formative organisation." Now, let's work with this for a second. Or let's go backwards. By this point -- by this point, the Territorial Defences have -- the weapons in the Territorial Defences have been siphoned off by the JNA. There are no more weapons to speak of.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are. I'm trying to assist you, but you won't listen to me. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We're talking about weapons that are being kept in -- not weapons being kept in the Territorial Defence warehouses, wherever they may be. We're talking about weapons that are being kept in public companies; correct? That's what this document is referring to.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, they don't want the JNA to get a hold of whatever little is left in Bosnia-Herzegovina, hence -- hence --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, we; the members of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. You, the president -- you, the Presidency, don't want the JNA to get what little is left, and so you come up with this idea. First, you declare that the weapons aren't safe where they're kept, that is, in the -- in the companies.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the JNA want to take them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. So it's not that there's -- that they're not safe there or that technical conditions for keeping the weapons -- you know, is not a safe place. That's just an excuse, and that's why you pass this decision to say, okay, let's give the weapons to MUP, because that's what's going to happen. It's really never going to go to the JNA warehouse. First it has to stop at MUP. This way, Bosnia and Herzegovina can begin to at least establish a -- a police force with -- with the little weapons it has left.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only for that reason, but also because it was only the police at that time that was allowed to have weapons. The police was under the leadership of the civilian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So that's what I wanted to cover, that in June the government itself, not having any of the choice, is going to turn over the weapons that are stored in the companies and give them to -- to --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not our government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not our government. It was the Communist government that did this before we came to power. I spoke about this yesterday. Both Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic. Mr. Kljuic, let's not play games. We're talking about the Presidency. It says here "the government of SRBiH." Okay? I don't care who put them there to begin with. The point I'm trying to drive home to this Tribunal is by this point there is no -- there is no army in BiH; correct? There is no Bosnia and Herzegovina army; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you have to find another witness to confirm what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must tell you that the key issue is the following: Before the democratic elections in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Communist governments handed over the weapons of the Territorial Defence to the JNA with the exception of individual companies. Unlike what Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina had done, Slovenia did not do this and, therefore, it had weapons to defend itself. So when you say the government, you can't say our government. We were faced with empty weapons depots because the Communists were afraid that if they lost the elections, the ownership of the weapons would change.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We are able to follow what you are saying, but you talk about the meeting you held at the Presidency. Are we to understand that the weapons were handed over to the JNA, that in the firms there are still a number of weapons that have been left, and the number you quoted only related to those weapons which were still to be found in -- in those public firms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Sorry to interrupt, but I was just going back to the transcript. Perhaps I missed it, but what kind of weapons and companies are we talking about? I've heard no explanation. Are we talking about the director's personal firearm or -- what kinds of guns and what volume are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's an excellent question. It's an excellent question and one must wonder why hasn't the Prosecutor asked the question. I will ask it for them because they ought to know by now, it's their case. What kind of weapons --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's your cross-examination, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's your case, sir. You indicted these folks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So, sir, what kind of weapons were left?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, the Territorial Defence had light weapons, short and long barrels. To a lesser extent there were bazookas, mortars, but those were smaller weapons intended for guerrilla warfare. There were no tanks, cannons, or things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And one last -- one last question: Why were the weapons kept there? I mean, there were warehouses, but why were they -- these -- certain weapons were kept in these companies.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was based on the Doctrine of Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know. I just wanted to get the answer from you so we -- so we all know, because under the Doctrine of Territorial Defence, everything was commandeered in case of a war. Everybody was mobilised. All the industries were mobilised. That was part of the essence of the Doctrine of the All People's Defence. Isn't that a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But every able-bodied person had weapons in the company they worked in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Okay. With that, we're going to move to another chapter. We've covered to some extent some points in this. I'm going to call this staffing policy problems in staffing. And let me preface my questions by saying earlier we talked about how difficult it was to staff certain positions in light of the transition with the new -- with the elections. There was a need to make certain appointments in various places based on proportional basis. Remember we had that conversation?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, for the record, I don't want to go through all the documents. I have several of them, but to save some time, and just for the record, in P 00027, which was introduced, we will find matters to that effect. P 0034 -- P 00034. P 00036. Let's look at that for a second. If we could pull that one up. This is on 29 May, 1991. The previous documents were from January 29 and 16 of April, 1991. Do you have the document in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You do not see it or you see it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the title of the document. I don't see the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, slowly we'll get it to you. All right. Now, if we could look at -- we're going to focus our attention on page 2, item 2, paragraph 1. In the B/C/S version it would be page 2, item 2, paragraph 1. They coincide. So with the usher's assistance ... Here we're going to talk a little bit about the problems. Item 2, it says here: "The deputies in the BiH Assembly who were elected by the HDZ are obliged to attend the scheduled sessions of the Assembly and the HDZ Deputies' Club." Let me stop there for a second. Isn't it a fact, sir, that at that point in time it was rather difficult for you as party -- as president of the party, because a lot of the delegates, a lot of deputies were not attending sessions or leaving sessions, and that had been a constant theme within some of the meetings, of how to get folks to do their job?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had the president of their Deputies' Club who was in charge of seeing whether they were coming, whether they were sticking to the agenda, and so on. But in spite of this, people didn't turn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And if you -- we don't need to go through the entire item 2, but just if you skip to the paragraph 3, it says that some deputies are irresponsible. And it goes on and on. What I'm trying to point out is it was a very difficult time. Some folks that were elected to positions did not take them seriously.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at item 4, item 4 in -- I believe it's -- it would be page -- page 3, I believe, or page 4 in the B/C/S. But let's look at item 4, paragraph 4. That would be page 4, sir.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. Point 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in the English version it would be on page 4, and if I can read it: "The Municipal Boards and the city board of the BH HDZ shall submit a written report on the progress made in assuming power in the municipalities and the problems that arise. The boards should also submit a report on their staffing requirements so that a redistribution of personnel can be made at the republican level." And then further down, if you skip one paragraph, it says: "The competent authorities shall speed up the appointment of executive personnel at the republican level, bearing in mind the territorial representation of personnel." So here we are, 29 May, 1991, and it appears that, based on these minutes, that appointments are slow to come, perhaps because you're having a hard time finding qualified people or people who are willing to participate in HDZ politics, as you indicated earlier.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to go -- let's go to another document, and that would be 00041, 10 July, 1991, a few months later. If we could have that. And I'm going to focus your attention on page 3, item 2(c). In the B/C/S, it would be page 3, and I'll read it and see if you can follow along: "Some deputies representing the HDZ do not attend BH Assembly sessions, attend them irregularly, or leave the Assembly early. In the future, such behaviour shall not be tolerated, especially since lately the Assembly has been debating crucial decisions." And if we go up a little bit, we'll see that you're mentioned as head of the Security Council within the HDZ. So that was the situation as it was back then, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. I apologise for interrupting, but I just have to wonder, are these -- are these the questions that should really justify possibly bringing this man back on another -- having him come back to The Hague on another occasion? Are these really the most important questions to put to this witness? And I wonder, what about the other Defence counsel? What is the allocation of their time --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I respond as to the relevancy, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Karnavas. What is the purpose of the questions you're asking now? You now said you would talk about appointments. What are you trying to demonstrate?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The relevance of the questioning is as follows: The gentleman had testified on direct examination that he was more or less forced out of the party. There are a lot of documentation here showing that there was discontent within the leadership with Mr. Kljuic, rightly or wrongly, that in one area at least, with the appointments, they were too slow to come and that the party wasn't organised properly and things weren't working. So part -- the Prosecution, at least as I understood it, was advocating that within this joint criminal enterprise there were those who were working against this particular gentleman, and I -- what I am putting is that there was just some dissatisfaction, and as in any political party, sometimes there are misunderstandings, but in this instance there were some reasons why those within the political leadership felt that Mr. Kljuic wasn't responding enough. Now, he's given us reasons how difficult it was, and I think we have to take him at his -- at his word. But the point is there's no joint criminal enterprise to force him out in order to conduct some nefarious affairs later on. That's the point that I'm trying to make. Now, if the Prosecutor wants to concede that point, then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we've got the point. Ask him the question, and tell him that he had to leave the party, and you have some evidence to prove this, that he left the party because he didn't manage things well and things were running late. And in that case, he will respond and say either it's true or it isn't. And we save time. What we need is to -- we need to understand the relevance here and understand in which way it is useful to you and in which way it contradicts the arguments put forward by the Prosecution. I think things are quite clear now, aren't they, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just waiting for the translation. Sorry, I'm just waiting for the translation. Very briefly, Your Honour. First of all, to respond to Mr. Karnavas about the relevancy of this, I think -- I don't think that the transcript of the 27th of December, 1991, meeting had anything to do with whether some people were attending sessions or not in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The disagreement between this man and others in the party was quite clear and it had a lot more to do with other things besides whether people showed up for certain meetings or not. Secondly, Your Honour, again I think -- if that's -- if that's Mr. Karnavas's -- as you said, Mr. President, and I fully agree with you, if that's Mr. Karnavas's case, he should put that case directly to the witness. "Sir, isn't it true that the real reason you were removed from office was administrative incompetence," what have you, but put the question directly to the witness instead of spending the next three hours talking about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours -- Your Honours -- if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the question that should be asked. Like that, we all save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I dare say -- I dare say that is not how to conduct cross-examination. It may be for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In your country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Even in this country, sir. Even in this country. Because there are a lot of documents here and the situation is extremely complex. There's not just one issue. There were lots of issues why there was dissatisfaction. Now, if the Court wishes me to move on, very well, I'll move on, I'll state for the record the documents I wanted to go through. These are documents of the Prosecution case. I'm entitled to lay the groundwork. Otherwise, everybody will miss the point, and I think there's been some benefit by having this gentleman go into a great deal of the details because the situation is rather complex. And so it's not easy to always ask the direct question. Sometimes you have to lay a foundation. So -- but I can just state for the record, based on all the documents that were available to us from the Prosecution with respect to dissatisfaction within the party or with the slowness in making appointments, I will read for the record the documents that I was going to go through and then I will close this chapter and move on to another. All right? So, first document, as I indicated, would be P 00027. Second document is P 00034. Next document, P 00036. We just covered that. P 00041, P 00045, P 00082, P 00116, P 09616. These are the documents. And might I also add that because the Prosecutor is introducing so many documents and since the Tribunal here under these particular rules allow all these documents to come in without laying a foundation, it is necessary at times for me to question a witness with respect to documents. I'm fully mindful of the rules we have here, and the Rules of Evidence. So I'm labouring under extreme, difficult conditions. Maybe not as difficult as Mr. Kljuic had, but nonetheless they're difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I have to respond to that. It's Mr. Karnavas -- every time there's a criticism or a question about Mr. Karnavas, of course it always -- the blame is always shifted to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "The reason I can't conduct a more effective cross-examination, that I repeat the same question seven or eight, nine times, is because there's so many documents in the Prosecution case." Your Honour, we moved through these documents quite efficiently. I believe the record will show that, and again that is not my fault for Mr. Karnavas's cross-examination. And I object, and on behalf of the entire Prosecution team, Your Honour, I resent that every time Mr. Karnavas has a problem in the courtroom, of course it's always blamed on the Prosecution. We have a standing objection to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to -- I will move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well -- Mr. Karnavas, you have mentioned a number of documents. You have given us some examples contained in some of these documents, so I think you could now ask the vital question. So put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And there's the little problem. I will do so, Your Honour, but that's why I have to show them the documents. But nonetheless, I will -- I will go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I read, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can introduce another document which will be a clear example of the point you would wish to make. Last time you weren't here, your colleague, when it came to talking about renaming of documents -- renaming of street names that were no longer Croatian street names, I think 10 or so examples were given. We're just trying to save time. So you have a document and you can say with this document we can illustrate what happened. But I think that is enough. Suffice to just use one document. I understand that you may need four to five days if you proceed this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm just trying to be thorough, Your Honour, and I take -- I take the -- the advice of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could -- if we could look at one document, 11 -- P 00116. And while we're looking at this -- for this document, sir, you've been following the discussion.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And would it be fair to say that one of the criticisms that had been lodged against you, among many other - and I'm not saying that they're justified - but as you said some folks were impatient, some were operating with less knowledge, some didn't quite appreciate the difficulties you had, but was it not one of the frustrations or one of the complaints that you were moving too slow on the appointment process?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer you, I wish to say that it's not true what you said a little while ago, that I was expelled from the HDZ. I resigned on the 2nd of February, 1992, and that's the truth. There are documents to prove that. As for criticism of myself and whether I was slow or not, you have to know what the context was. A change in the state system, people who hadn't been checked, and the opposition that you're standing by now would show the results later on, when I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I apologise -- I apologise if the impression was that you were expelled. I'm not suggesting that, the Prosecution is suggesting that. And so if we could look at page 5 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that I was expelled, excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, we're going to get to your resignation. Okay? We will get there. We talked about -- by the way, we did talk about earlier how, at least on a different matter, you believed, as you testified under oath in Kordic, that you had been expelled or you had lost your position or dismissed, call it whatever you will, from the Presidency, and this was as a result of President Tudjman cutting a deal with President Izetbegovic, because this would allow Izetbegovic to unconstitutionally remain in power as president of the Presidency beyond the two-year limitation; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when it came -- now, getting back to the issue. If you look at page 5, at the bottom -- in English it's page 5. It's titled "Re-examination of Staff Appointments." I don't know if it corresponds with your document, sir, the page number, but at the top of the page it would be 00533966. That might assist the -- the usher. And it says here: "The competent bodies of HDZ BH are to immediately collect written approvals from the HDZ municipal boards responsible for all staff on a local level appointed to represent the HDZ of BiH. Those who do not receive the approval must immediately have dismissal procedures initiated against them while the appointment of new staff should proceed according to the regulated procedure. A candidate who is not a member of the HDZ cannot be appointed to a post in the bodies of the republic. All the HDZ municipal boards of BH and the HDZ Presidency of BH are requested to take up the portfolios which had been assigned to them in the distribution of portfolios." Now, that was the policy back then, was it not? HDZ, the political party, was the one that was entrusted in filling those positions.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the composition of the government, the ministers, something that had to be decided straight away, any subsequent appointment was at the proposal of the cadres commission. Now, the fact that some people didn't like the fact that we had put in people who weren't active members of the party but were experts was natural. However, I was not able to appoint somebody to a particular post, or the cadres commission people to a particular post if they didn't have any experience or qualifications for the job. And from this we can clearly see that what they wanted was that every person first be a party member, then he must be put forward by a municipal organisation, and once he's verified by the municipal organisation, he gains the necessary credibility. First of all, we didn't have time to do all that. Secondly, we -- people didn't want to take up posts. What use would it be to put someone forward if the person didn't want to occupy a state function? So that there were many personal family-tie combinations and so on I have to say that I couldn't pay attention, take all this into account at the time, all the more so as I wasn't personally responsible, it was always the commission that was responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because you were the head of the party, a lot of the criticism was coming back to you, whether you deserved it or not; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But from these manuscripts you can see which group of people were against me and how their voice grew louder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, within the same document, on a slightly different issue but still voices of discontent, if we look on page 4 - and for the B/C/S version it would be on page 00533965 - it says here: "The assessment of the work and the role of the party. The attitude of the Croatian representatives in BiH Assembly, especially when the issue of referendum was being decided is a direct result of the absence of a clear political stance, which is an unacceptable political improvisation of the leadership of HDZ of BiH. Before having reached such an essential decision, consultation with the competent bodies of the party should have been conducted, which was not done at any level. The work of the party is otherwise assessed to be poor, disorganised, motivated by private issues and political -- and politically irresponsible, which will not be permitted in future." Now, to some extent, sir, it would appear that there's a little criticism being lodged against you in this. Rightly or wrongly. I'm not suggesting that it's correct. I'm just saying that at least from the document, on its face, that there were -- there was blame -- you were being blamed for a variety of reasons.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, very rarely do you have an international document that can stand the test of 15 years' time, and you're asking for a digest from the minutes of a party that had just been established to be absolutely correct and exact and something that one could rely on. Now, you see here when people say that the deputies were wrong in voting for the referendum question as set by the republican commission, don't wish to understand that in our programme declaration the first principle was a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina and the equality of Croats within it. So those two principles are -- were contained in that question. Now, I assume that the person speaking here said that they should be convened and then told don't vote now, we're going to prepare the Livno issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here, because I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, may I add for a point of the witness. Are you saying, Witness, that this criticism is not serious, was not even seriously brought forward but was masking other aversion against you? Is that what you're putting forward?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The criticism was serious. It wasn't a trick. Those people really wanted that. However, the criticisms were not because of my work but because I, as a political figure, with absolute legitimacy, got in their way. And we were to solve that two or three days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I think you touched upon a problem that I wanted to cover within this global aspect, which was how difficult it was starting -- starting with this new -- new system, elections, formation of parties, and would it be fair to say that many folks had unrealistic expectations?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would put it this way: They had -- they had unrealistic assessments, not expectations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Assessments. And some of these unrealistic assessments came back to haunt you personally because you were criticised.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I believe we covered that point. If I could just move on to another chapter, and this has to do with -- I'm trying to clarify a point that was raised yesterday -- oh, I apologise, and I'll try to move faster too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's time to take a break. It's half past 3.00. So in theory, we should reconvene in 20 minutes and go on working until 5.30. Will you all have finished by 5.30, or do you think we're going to have to have the witness back, Mr. Karnavas? How much more time do you need, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm trying to move fast, as fast as I can. I will look at -- I will look over at the break to see what I can do, and I do want to clarify one thing at the point. I think it's an unfair characterisation, Judge Trechsel, to say that I'm cross-examining as if I was in the United States. Trust me, I'm not. I've modified completely my approach. I'm trying to adjust. It's a little bit difficult, but I take your point to heart. I will try to be as precise as possible, and I thank you for the criticism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I apologise if you felt offended. This was certainly not my intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You must know that they're not criticisms on the part of the Judges, they're just observations in order to try and make our work more efficacious on all sides. So no criticisms, just observations to give you food for thought. So the problem is as follows: We're going to work this evening until 5.30. Is the Defence -- will the Defence be finished by 5.30 and so that we can let the witness go, or are we going to have to recall the witness? Because if the Prosecution has redirect, then we won't have time. Mr. Scott, do you intend to ask additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me answer your question this way, Your Honour, in terms of where we are: I frankly had intended, at the beginning of the last session, to raise this question and decided not to interrupt and hope that maybe perhaps Mr. Karnavas would be concluding early in the last session, so I decided not to interrupt. I suppose it's almost a fait accompli now, perhaps, that the witness will have to come back. I must say I don't think there has been a wise use of the cross-examination time so far --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object to those comments, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think other counsel, Defence counsel should, of course, have an opportunity, a reasonable opportunity to put questions to the witness, but now we find ourselves at a time where the Prosecution -- and I'll certainly be governed by the Registry's time, but according to our estimates, we used approximately five hours and 36 minutes. The Defence so far has had right at five hours, and except for a few minutes by Mr. Ibrisimovic, that has all been taken by Mr. Karnavas, and I just say I just say that I think it's a bit of a shame that the witness will have to come back when I think that the time today could have been used more wisely. Secondly, to answer your question, Your Honour, if we could finish today in order to accommodate the witness, I would be happy not to ask any questions on redirect. Of course, if the witness does come back, then likely there will be some redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a court of justice. Now, if these gentlemen are going to get a fair trial, they are entitled to their share. Now, the Prosecutor ought to be ashamed of himself of presenting the case the way he's presenting it. He's dumping documents and now he's saying that I should just forego my client's rights because of some time schedule that he has. Madam Del Ponte came here and said she doesn't want to cut. Why should I give up my client's rights to accommodate the Prosecutor? No way. I'm entitled to ask these questions. This is a very complicated issue. This witness was at the forefront of the events. He's a critical witness, and I think every issue that we're covering is relevant. My colleagues fully agree with me. They have their own space, and they're entitled to as much time as they need, and as I'm told, they're going to need, collectively, about three or four hours. And I think -- I forewarned everyone in advance that I needed about six hours. Now, I will try to do my best. That's the best I could do. But I will not accept any criticism from Mr. Scott especially, especially when I see how he's presenting his case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. During the break you're going to see each other, and if we finish by 5.30, well and good. If not, we're going to continue at a subsequent date. And I'd like to ask the registrar to give me a breakdown of the time used. So we'll do those sums. Judge Prandler would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would simply like to say that again there should be avoiding any expression which is in a way offending anybody; offending either the witness, either the Defence, or the Prosecution. And we heard now a few minutes ago that the Prosecution should be ashamed of himself or itself. I really feel that these kind of expressions are to be avoided. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that my Defence counsel has the right to defend me, and please allow my Defence counsel to do his work. The witness said that none of us took part, but because of the character of the indictment, we have to address all these matters. So we are the party in jeopardy, those of us sitting here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's 20 to 4.00. We're taking a break and we're going to reconvene at approximately 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I'd like to make an observation with respect to time. We've been doing the calculations. Mr. Scott has used five hours and 40 minutes, and today the Defence used five hours, 20 minutes so far. So pursuant to our decision that the time should be equally shared unless it was the personal responsibility of the people, that the same time should be accorded to both the Prosecution and the Defence. So that's the framework. Mr. Karnavas, please continue. Could you tell us whether you have discussed the matter with your other colleagues and what the outcome is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Briefly, we've consulted with each other, and here's where it stands: I'm going to continue with my cross-examination. It will probably -- not probably, it will, indeed, take the rest of the time. I'm hoping to finish by that point in time. And I understand that the Stojic team has approximately an hour and a half. I know General Praljak would like to -- has some questions of about half an hour, slightly more, perhaps slightly less. I know the Petkovic team has approximately an hour to an hour and a half, and I understand the Coric team has approximately 30 minutes to 45 minutes. That's where we stand, Your Honour, and again I want to remind the Court that this deals with joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You forgot -- yes, go ahead, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wanted to say that we would need one and a half hours, not 30 to 40 minutes, as was stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I stand corrected. So there we are. There we are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think our colleague managed to collect all the relevant information. We had to adjust our time. General Praljak's Defence will need about an hour at the minimum, as things now stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And 15 minutes for General Praljak within that hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. As things now stand, General Praljak will use up a whole hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Him? Very well. That means that the witness will have to come back another day. So we're going to finish the sitting today with Mr. Karnavas. We have until 5.30. And then, sir, you will have to come back at a future date which is convenient to you, and the cross-examination will last another morning or afternoon, because usually a sitting is four hours and 45 minutes, a day's sitting. So that means one more day of sitting, an additional day, and that will get through it. Mr. Karnavas, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe Mr. Murphy wanted to say something. I saw him stand up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I just wanted to make a modest contribution, Your Honour, to diminishing the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your contribution is never modest, Mr. Murphy. It is always highly important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. A modest contribution to the -- the scope of the indictment, perhaps, by correcting the record at page 91, line 2, which talks about weapons being acquired for the protection of the Croatian people from September 1891 to 1991. I think if we narrow that down to 1991, Your Honour, it may save a great deal of time. I ask for the record to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, fine. Thank you. I took note of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could now move on to another chapter, and this would be clarifying the -- some issues with respect to the two different versions of the decision that was shown to you yesterday, the decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So first, to recap, yesterday you were shown a document, I believe it was 1D -- well, 1D 00048 -- 1D 00488. I don't know. The Prosecution's document might have been -- I don't know what the number is, but that's the document that we have. This was the original, the initial decision, if you see it. Do you see it, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All you need to see is the first part of it. I have -- I have a copy for you, a hard copy. One for the ELMO, one for you. This was the document that was shown to you yesterday, sir, was it not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That stated that on 18 November, 1991, there was a decision passed. Now, if you will recall, there was another document with the same title, different date, and this was Prosecution Exhibit 00078, and that's the one that shows that the 18 -- that the decision of 18 November, 1991, had been amended.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. To assist the Court - excuse me - the document on the screen now is the same as document P 00081.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it was yesterday you were asked to look at it, and I believe yesterday we were able to determine that some changes had been made; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can see in front of me is the decision of the 18th. 18th of November, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could pull up the 00078 for the gentleman. And you will see from the preamble where it says: "The decision to establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was adopted by the elected representatives of the Croatian people at the session held on 18 November, 1991. The said decision was amended at the session of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna on 3 July, 1992, and the final draft reads as follows." Do you see that one, sir? It's at the very, very top of the page. If it's not there, sir, we can provide you with a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. And yesterday we had this discussion, and -- you had a discussion with respect to this particular document, a discussion generated by the Prosecution wherein you said that you took exception to this particular decision because it appeared that they had taken on executive powers; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you look on -- if you look at Article 7. If you compare Article 7 of the first document with Article 7 in the amended version, I believe, based on viewing Article 7 and then Article 8, I believe you had some reservations with respect to this particular decision. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first decision was taken while it was still peacetime. The second, of the 3rd of July, 1992, was made during the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now you say peacetime, but we went through all these documents. That was the essence of this entire exercise, even though the aggression hadn't formally started, it was clear that war was about to start or Bosnia-Herzegovina was about to be attacked; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was what was assumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And now you rightly noted that several months later, 3 July, 1992, war has broken out and the situation on the ground has changed markedly; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
