utterances.text: Now, with that in mind, perhaps we can go through the chronology of the major events that took place during that gap, and that might assist the Trial Chamber, and the Prosecution and anybody else who might be listening, to know what exactly took place during those months and perhaps why it was necessary to amend that decision, okay? So --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- I'm going to go through a series of dates and events, and if you could just say "yes" or "no," or "I don't know," I would most appreciate it, but this is the chronology that I put on. We'll move rather quickly. 18 November, 1991, that's the first document, but also that is the date where Vukovar is in the hands of the Serbs; right? Rather memorable date, 18 November.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 23 December, 1991, Germany recognises Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 30 December, 1991, 700.000 refugees and displaced persons find themselves in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 9 January, 1992, the Republika Srpska, the RS, is established within BiH.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it wasn't legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree with you there. Probably, but nonetheless it was established; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. 15 January, 1992, the EU recognises the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 9 January, 1992, this is -- there's a meeting of the Central Board of HDZ Livno, and that had to do with a question that we talked about. Remember we had that lengthy discussion? We'll move on because we covered that already. On 28 February --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, sorry. The 9th of February, if I can just correct that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 9th of February, 1992, there was the meeting in Livno, and we had this whole discussion. And since this is on the record, we need not cover it. On the 28th of February and March 1, 1992, we have the referendum about the independence of the SRBiH; correct? Those are the dates when people went out and voted.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The 29th. Thank you very much. It was a late night last night, trying to get this together. March 25, 1992, Neum is shelled by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And Neum, for those of us who haven't been there, is right on the coast. It's one of the few -- that little bitty coast that's been allocated or that belongs to BiH of the entire Adriatic coast. It's about 10 kilometres long.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. 29 -- 29 March, 1992, people, Croats -- Croats and Muslims, several thousand, from South Herzegovina are escaping to West Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 30 March, 1992, people from North Bosnia are escaping to the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 2nd of April, 1992, Bijeljina, which is a town, as you well know, in -- in Bosnia and Herzegovina, is under siege by Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, crimes happened over there on that day as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. In fact, there's some footage. I believe it was Arkan that goes there and commits all those crimes. In fact, it was videotaped. But it was at this particular time, as I recall, that Alija Izetbegovic, the president of the SDA, who is also the president of the Presidency, states, "I think that we cannot say that we have a war in SRBiH. Clashes will stop as soon as BiH is recognised on 7 of April, 1992." Do you recall him saying that? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly he said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And again, if indeed he had said that, little comfort was he giving to his own people, his own nation, let alone the Croats, if he's saying when Bijeljina is under siege, Arkan is going there, the notorious Arkan, and he's saying, "Well, we cannot say that we have a war in SRBiH." Moving along. 3rd of April, 1992, one day later, massacre in Bijeljina -- in Bijeljina mosque, Tuzla and Brcko under siege by Serb forces, Serbs take over Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, for those of us who don't know exactly where these places are, Brcko in particular, that's -- we're talking about the Posavina corridor, isn't it? It's right on there.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that place is going to play a very significant role, because if we were to look on the map of Bosnia and Herzegovina as it is today with the two entities, we'll see why Brcko is so important that at Dayton it was not resolved and had to go to international arbitration and was resolved three years later through an international arbitration award; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because if, for instance, Brcko -- Brcko, that corridor, would cut the RS in half. That's why Brcko was so important; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In Tuzla, Tuzla, which is -- has -- is historic in many ways for being a very multi-ethnic and tolerant city, and in fact during the war it stayed that way, more or less.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: April 4, 1992, general mobilisation is pronounced in the RS -- the SRBiH. Although we don't know by whom, general mobilisation was pronounced, if you will. 4 April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 5 April, 1992, Serbs started armed force conflict in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 6 April, 1992, the EU recognises BiH.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Same day in Sarajevo, extraordinary situation is pronounced. Extraordinary situation is pronounced.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In Mostar and Siroki Brijeg, shelling from North Camp by the GNA -- the JNA. Same day.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. The next day, 7 April, 1992, Republic of Croatia recognises BiH.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Serb members, on that same day, leave the Presidency of BiH.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. They had previously suspended or frozen their status. This was a trick. If they walked out of the Presidency, we would have the right, based on the constitution, to find replacements for them. It was quite clear, because after the elections there was a list, but by suspending their membership they were attempting to block the work of the Presidency. However, on the 7th, they all went over to Pale and then the crisis of the composition of the Presidency arose, which was solved in the subsequent period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. On that same day, 7 April, 1992, Medjugorje and Citluk are shelled by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this is sort of the first reaction by Izetbegovic against the JNA. It was on that day, 7 April, 1992, finally, Mr. Izetbegovic reacted as president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On the next day -- on next day, 8 April, 1992, the HVO -- the HVO is established as the supreme defence body; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: April 9 -- April 9, next day, decision on pronouncement of imminent war, imminent threat of war. And by doing so -- and by doing so, the Presidency has Assembly powers. That's what happens when the Presidency pronounced the imminent threat of war on 9 April, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the work of the Assembly was paralysed. It was no longer possible to work in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. And I'm trying to show what happened during these events. And so we can see now the Assembly is paralysed, and so the Presidency takes on its powers. Now, 11 April, 1992, Mostar comes under heavy shelling, does it not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every day, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to get there slowly, slowly, step-by-step.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. Mr. President, before it leaves the screen, I just wonder if the witness could assist us. On page 139 at line 3, Mr. Karnavas asks the question, "And this is sort of the first reaction by Izetbegovic," et cetera, but I don't see any description there of what this first reaction supposedly was. Maybe I missed it, but perhaps the witness could give us a full answer as to what this reaction supposedly was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Gladly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recall what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- his reaction was?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm asking you. You're the witness.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, this is a whole sea of events. This is not a quiz. You have to tell me what the statement was and I'll tell you whether I recognise it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We'll move on, Your Honour, and we'll establish that point through other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On 14 April, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, if you know how Mr. Izetbegovic reacted, you can ask him how he reacted and then the witness can respond and say yes, I corroborate this, or I don't. If you know. If you don't know, move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The reaction, as I understand, is a public condemnation against JNA.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we talked about the 11th, the shelling of Mostar. On the 14th of April, there's fighting in the city of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but I have to tell you you're listing one event after another, and these events occurred in a condensed period of time. I was a witness to all this, and I received information, but today, after so much time has elapsed, I cannot tell you whether something happened on the 14th or the 11th. I can tell you, generally speaking, that the whole territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially Sarajevo and the neighbourhoods inhabited by Croats and Bosniaks, were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Is Sarajevo under siege from 5 April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo was under siege even before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even during peacetime. The JNA officially held training exercises, and during that period it encircled Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But once it becomes even more under siege, as of on or about 5 April, 1992, would it be fair to say that Sarajevo in essence is cut off from the rest of the country because it's under siege?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the state -- the state institutions, such as they were at the time, were handicapped, unable, perhaps, to carry out many of their functions with respect to the rest of the country.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they couldn't carry out all their tasks. Everything was done to carry out what was possible. There were some secret routes one could use to get out of Sarajevo. We still had telephones and fax machines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Were there any problems with the central bank and the currency at the time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That problem had arisen much earlier, when the Republic of Croatia and, before that, Slovenia stopped using the Yugoslav dinar. We also took steps to print our own currency, but unfortunately, it remained in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that all the Yugoslav dinars from Croatia and Slovenia poured into Bosnia-Herzegovina, and its value was nothing. And then in Sarajevo we printed some sort of vouchers, and from that time onwards practically the only real currency in Bosnia-Herzegovina was the West German mark. And in memory of this, our currency today is called the mark, only it's called the convertible mark because it can be exchanged for other currencies in any bank in Bosnia and Herzegovina without any difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So for all intents and purposes, once the central bank stops operating, the currency that you've printed is left in London in some printing house, all you have are these sort of vouchers, as you've said, as somewhat of and official currency, or something to trade with, but certainly nothing that you can take outside and trade for -- for marks or dollars, guilders, or what have you.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had nothing. But you have to know that in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a lot of people had worked abroad, and for many years the dinar had not been convertible; there were a lot of German marks around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That I understand. I just want to make sure that the Trial Chamber understood that in this period of time there is no official currency, nothing that's functioning in the -- in the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Not that anyone's fault, other than the war and the circumstances that were placed upon Bosnia-Herzegovina by the former Yugoslavia, primarily from events occurring from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one example. If you told us that at the time you were in Sarajevo when you went out to buy some bread, what did you pay for your bread with? Was it a Belgrade dinar or a voucher or German marks? When you went out to buy something, what kind of currency did you use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had both vouchers and marks, but most people had vouchers, but after the aggression started, bread was distributed free of charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These vouchers, did they resemble banknotes? Was there a nominal value to these vouchers or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They resembled theatre tickets or tickets for sports events. They had various nominal values, but we had to abolish them very soon because people falsified them. They forged them. They printed them out on their computers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who issued these -- these vouchers? Was this the state? Was this done through the state bank, the central bank?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, actually, it was the central bank, but it was actually the state that was responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I've heard, and I'm not prepared to -- to go forward on this today, but I've heard that certain municipalities also printed their own money, or had their own way of bartering -- their own bartering system with similar vouchers. I could be wrong, but is there any truth to that? If you know.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're right. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I thought so. And would you care -- I mean, just from memory, if you can tell us some of those places that were printing their own vouchers or sort of currency, whatever you want to call it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I do know it was the practice. I was in Sarajevo. I didn't leave Sarajevo for a long time, but I know that the problem was solved in the same way as in Sarajevo. People printed some sort of vouchers or papers on the basis of which one could get a litre of oil or a kilo of sugar or a loaf of bread or powdered milk or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just an additional question. Were salaries paid in vouchers, of state employees and others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but very few people received salaries. At that time, as a member of the Presidency, I earned one German mark a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, moving along on our chronology. And incidentally, if you don't remember, say you don't remember, or you think it's correct, just say you think. It's behooves the Defence to prove up all of these dates, which we intend to do throughout the course of this trial. So on the 16th of April, 1992, Mostar is bombarded from the North Camp. Do you recall that? And from another --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. On 18th of April, 1992, Sarajevo is heavily attacked.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On April 21, 1992, Alija Izetbegovic is calling the inhabitants of Sarajevo to defend Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I called on them on the 4th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And as I understand it -- one second, with your indulgence. Let me move on here. On -- on the 26th of April, 1992, do you recall whether Mate Boban issued a letter concerning Mr. Izetbegovic's response?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, but I know they communicated with each other because two days later they went to a conference in Lisbon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps we could pull up 1D 00525. And I have hard copies in the event you can't see it on the screen because, as I understand, it's a poor copy, and we may need -- If we could take the other document from the -- sir, if we could take the document off the ELMO as well. And this is for the ELMO. This is in English. And if you could just give it a quick read. I'm primarily interested in the third paragraph, third and fourth paragraph. And here we have -- For the record, paragraph 3 says: "Still convinced that the principles of the negotiations under the patronage of the European Community are the only possible way for establishing -- for the establishing of the Government of the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina that the war still can be stopped, it is necessary to apply at once some of the agreed principles of the future constitutional arrangements of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that perhaps -- since this is dated April 26, it would appear that he's referring to the earlier document that we saw earlier, back in March, the one that was in the text that was shown to you that we talked about.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'll get the number for the record on that. And for the record, that was 1D 00398, what we were referring to earlier as the -- the Statement of Principles of 18 March, 1992. Then it goes on to say: "Therefore, we suggest, that instead of disintegrated and illegal authorities, immediately a Ministry Council of Bosnia and Herzegovina should be mandated, consisting of nine members (a party of the three people) as the European Community has proposed, being the only authority of temporary governing Bosnia and Herzegovina." So here's Boban making this proposal as president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to Mr. Cutileiro, Izetbegovic -- and he's copying Izetbegovic and Karadzic. Were you aware of this, sir, of this initiative?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I knew about the meeting they had two days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But at least from here we -- it would suggest -- the text would suggest that Mate Boban, as president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, is reaching out, and he's making a proposal, and it seems that the proposal is suggesting a formula that would prevent war and ensure that all three peoples and their rights be guaranteed and assured. Would you not agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The witness has already said he knows nothing about this document whatsoever, so this is pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm asking the gentleman to comment based on the text and based on his knowledge of the events. I think that he can -- he's perfectly capable, particularly keeping in mind that we discussed the text of -- of 18 -- of 18 March, 1992. So the gentleman was in the Presidency at the time. If he's unable to answer, then he can certainly tell us that he's unable. I'll accept that and move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I submit that this is just again asking -- this is asking the witness to agree with one more of Mr. Karnavas's speeches. The witness has already said he doesn't have any knowledge about this effort by Mr. Boban at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm asking the witness to interpret the text. Now, if the Court wishes for me to move on, I'll move on. It's not a speech; it's a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Witness, please answer the question. The Defence is showing you a text in which Mr. Boban is suggesting to Mr. Cutileiro, Mr. Izetbegovic, and Karadzic, in other words, a constitution based on equal representation, and the issue of Bosnia-Herzegovina was addressed. As you were a member of the Presidency, were you aware of the content of this proposal? Yes or no. And an underlying question to this one: What was your feeling about such a proposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I didn't have this text. Secondly, it wasn't possible to stop the war. It had been planned much earlier. If one had wanted to stop the war and have a peaceful discussion about the constitutional reorganisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there wouldn't have been any shooting. And then in this proposal, it has been forgotten that Bosnia-Herzegovina is an independent state, and by proposing the establishment of a nine-member council, probably the assumption is that this would derogate the government and Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina as legally elected and brought into crisis after the departure of the Serbs, even though a number of Serbs did remain, especially in the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Nonetheless, I think what we can see is at least an initiative on the part of Mr. Boban in trying to find a solution, albeit rather creative, perhaps not realistic, but he is trying to make an effort of thinking outside the box under a most difficult situation when, as you've indicated, Sarajevo is not really functioning much and the state institutions, many of them are not functioning as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, we're back to making a speech again. There is just nothing more than Mr. Karnavas making an arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the gentleman has already answered these question. The concept is called looping, and I'm happy to give the gentleman a lesson afterwards, but that's what I'm doing. I'm looping his previous answers into my question. These are established facts. They come from the witness himself. They're not Karnavas making speeches. He's indicated that most of the institutions were not functioning. We talked about the currency, we talked about Sarajevo being under siege. What part of the question is a fact that is not in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Most all of it, Your Honour. I don't know what looping is. "Looping" is new term to me, Your Honour, but all it is is Mr. Karnavas following an answer and then restating it in a way that suits his argument. If the witness has answered the question, he's answered the question. It isn't up to Mr. Karnavas to recharacterise the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Karnavas, please move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You asked the witness what he felt about this proposal. He responded by saying that because it was wartime, it wasn't realistic and none of this could work. So this is the feeling we have. So please don't belabour the point. There might be more interesting questions you would like to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On the 27th of April, 1992, BiH Presidency rendered a decision that the JNA should leave Bosnia and Herzegovina, and on that same day the JNA is shelling -- or still shelling Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We as an independent state asked that a foreign army leave Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when was this independent state declared an independent state? Just if you could remind us again. Was it on that date?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The independent state? No. That was before. You know that on the 5th of April, President Tudjman recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina, and 74 countries of the world recognised it over the following few days. The European Community recognised it on the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Precisely. And my question is: What took the Presidency 19 days to finally say, "Hey, we've got a foreign occupying force here. Why don't you leave?" What was the purpose of allowing them 19 or 20 days to continue to wreak havoc and raise hell in Bosnia-Herzegovina? If you have the answer, give it to us. If not, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you something. You're looking at papers, and they don't provide you with a good picture of events. We couldn't walk around the town because of the JNA. One had to carry out some preparations, mobilise at least some services, especially the police, as far as it was possible, to ensure the work of the state bodies. Besides, we spoke to the representatives of the European Union who had arrived in Sarajevo and asked that the European Union, in recognising us, protect Bosnia-Herzegovina and eliminate the JNA from our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where none of this was successful, we then went public and sent a demand to Belgrade that they should withdraw an army which was a foreign army on our territory. But they didn't leave, and Belgrade had no intention of withdrawing it, and nobody in Europe cared about how we were managing to survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not quite answering the question. It seems like the European Union recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 6th of April. Why did you need to wait several days before warning the JNA that it needed to withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina? Why wait for so long? Is it because you trusted the European Union to settle the issue or, as you indicated, you were involved with other things like mobilisation of the police force and military equipment? Does that explain why you had to wait for such a long time? On the 27th of April, you called upon the JNA so that it withdraws from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you answer this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I can't answer it. I can't tell you the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. But I do appreciate the fact that you told us and you shared with us the difficulties in understanding the events by simply looking at paper. We need live testimony such as the one that we're getting here to convey the images of what was happening at the time. Now, please tell us whether on the 28th of April, 1992, the BiH Presidency pronounced Serbia as an aggressor.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And on the 29th, negotiations in Lisbon were taking place?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that, but I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. On the 30th of April, 1992, Mostar is still under the shelling of -- still under the shelling; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And then the republic Territorial Defence headquarters orders its units, whatever they are, to stand against the JNA. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then we're going to get to this date of the 2nd to 3rd of May, 1992, was a day when Alija Izetbegovic was some say arrested, others say he was kidnapped, others say that he was held, detained, whatever it may be. Do you recall that particular day? Especially since you, as I understand it, were one of the protagonists in that event.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if I -- if I could get the technical booth to assist us, we're going to look at a video. I suspect that it has a number. It does not have a number. But this was -- if we could look at it. And while it's getting -- we're getting ready, I must apologise for not having the text translated. We will get it translated. But if we could look at it first and then at some critical point we'll ask the witness to assist us with what is happening. And it's very short but rather interesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How long does the video last?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I understand it, less than -- less than a minute. It's ... The video itself, Your Honour, is when Izetbegovic was being detained. Apparently he was able to communicate and have live communications, and so that's what this is about. And as I understand it, and the gentleman can confirm, that he was in -- he was communicating with Mr. Izetbegovic as he was being held captive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when the Serbs allowed him to communicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But he was on the phone and you were speaking to him; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I think here it is. If we could slowly -- if we could look at this. This is President Izetbegovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. From the smile on your face --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would have been a good idea if the interpreters could have translated this. I -- usually they do. I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President, and it's one of those things that you come up against. You come up against deadlines, and this came to us late in the hour. I apologise, but perhaps we can get -- through my questioning we'll find out what happened, and we'll have it translated and we can show it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The question I would like to ask, and it's a question, a technical question, could we not have it run again and our interpreters, while it runs, interpret the text? Is that not possible? I think it would be better than if the witness were to translate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree. Your Honour, I agree. We could have the -- I have no problems with that. I've never -- because there's lots of talking going on, and I don't want to tax our good translators, but certainly, why not? Play it again and perhaps they can cue in and tell us whether they're able to do that. I'm not saying that they're not, so --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can do their best. However, if we don't have a transcript, we usually don't translate videos without a B/C/S transcript, because it's very fast and the voices overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the interpreters translate the video and listen to what's being said?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They -- I think at some point, but I know how difficult it is when they're speaking at this pace and you have interlapping. We will provide -- the most critical aspect, perhaps, of the tape that could be, and perhaps they could assist us with, is if we play it back and they play the section where Mr. Kljuic, at the end, is having a conversation with Mr. Izetbegovic, at which point Mr. Izetbegovic asks Mr. Kljuic to hand the phone over to Mr. Ganic. But we're going to cover this. If I could ask some questions first and it might -- and then we can perhaps go back to the video. If that may assist the Trial Chamber. And again I apologise, but this came to us literally, you know, overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps if you put the question to the witness how -- you could talk about the way in which he was arrested. We know nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Kljuic, I know it's been some time, but I take it, hearing yourself, seeing the events, brought back flashes of memory. On that particular day, as I indicated, Alija Izetbegovic was arrested or detained by the JNA. Could you tell us a little bit, but very briefly because we don't have that much time, but briefly, where was Mr. Izetbegovic at the time when he was detained?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was coming back from Lisbon, from the tripartite conference there. When he arrived at Sarajevo airport, instead of going to the Presidency, the Yugoslav People's Army arrested him. In the meantime, as there was a lot of shooting during those days and the defenders responded in like manner to the Yugoslav army, there was a situation in which the military command of the Sarajevo Corps, led by General Kukanjac, remained in an encirclement, under siege. However, his assistant and adjutant, General Djurdjevac, brought Izetbegovic to Lukavica - it's a large barracks outside town - and while this was going on, everybody was shooting. Most -- the worst thing was that the paramilitaries started firing, and they were firing at the Yugoslav People's Army in order to retaliate towards the citizens of Sarajevo. And now everybody stopped shooting. And while this was being confirmed on the Serb side, a shell fell in front of our windows and demolished the room we were in. However, Izetbegovic and us and Kukanjac, who was in the encirclement, asked that there be a cease-fire. There's an important fragment missing here where I told Izetbegovic that he mustn't sign anything because he had been taken into custody. However, he says at the end that Ganic was replacing him. Now, for you to understand that paradox, I have to tell you that during the Communist regime a series of changes had taken place in the Presidency. At its head there was a Serb, a Croat, a Muslim. That was the order within the Presidency. The last Communist president was a Serb. Now we had Izetbegovic, who used as much time as possible accorded to him by the constitution, under the constitution, and the next person was to have been me. Today in the Presidency we have the same order, but instead of seven members there are three. And today the practice is that if there is no presiding officer, the next person to be president and the next person in line replaces him. However, Izetbegovic said that Ganic would be replacing him, and I have to say that he did me a great service there because he was very fervent in replacing him, very enthusiastic, and negotiated, whereas in the meantime many crimes had been committed. Let me tell you something at this point. I'm a serious man, and I'm answering your questions and have been doing so for three days now. So please let me tell you something that I consider to be crucial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So he gave Ganic the authority to negotiate with UNPROFOR officers, because the programme was for Izetbegovic to be exchanged for Kukanjac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was Galic [as interpreted] a Croat, a Muslim, a Serb? What was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He's a Yugoslav. He was a Yugoslav. And in seven-member Presidency, he represented others, the other peoples. However, the command had to be pulled out, with all the soldiers and all the equipment, from Bistrik, which is a district of Sarajevo. And the representatives of UNPROFOR were there. Negotiations were held. I stayed in my room all the time, in my office, and then finally there was a truce, a cease-fire that was proclaimed for just a short while, 15 minutes. The firing stopped for 15 minutes, because we were in the centre of town and there was shooting coming from all sides, and Sarajevo is a city in a valley. So you don't have to see the shell but you can hear the echo and reverberation of a shell. And then it was envisaged that Izetbegovic from Lukavica, that is to say from the airport, which is called Lukavica, sets out for the command where Kukanjac was encircled so that they should go to the centre point in town, the Skenderija bridge, for Izetbegovic to turn right into the Presidency building and Kukanjac, with his entourage, officers, families, and so on, should go on further towards Lukavica which was the forward staff of the JNA. And at that point there was a lot of shooting. There were many casualties. Unfortunately, I wasn't there myself to be able to tell you exactly what happened, but politically speaking, after this solution - and this is something that the Croats held against him - because he told Ganic, "You replace me." That was more propaganda. The Croats weren't as sensitive where I was concerned, but that was the first sort of treachery of a multinational Bosnia-Herzegovina, where it had been betrayed. In the coming period, my position -- I would -- I -- I didn't hold it against Izetbegovic. I swallowed my pride, because what should I do, fight with the Muslims, argue with them? I didn't want to do so, because at that time the Muslim people were friendly towards us. But Izetbegovic was that kind of man. He didn't have trust or confidence in anyone, and the fact that it was contrary to the law at a time when there was shooting on all sides and when you did your best to save your skin, who cared whether it was Stjepan Kljuic according to protocol or somebody else. So I didn't take this in any tragic sense, although I never forgot what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now Ganic was a Muslim. He declared himself a Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But -- while you might not have taken offence -- hold on, sir. Let me pose the question. Okay. I'm let you -- you spoke for ten minutes on that one. Now, while Ganic -- while you didn't mind Izetbegovic passing you over, the Croatian people, of which you were representing at the Presidency level, saw that as a betrayal because you were passed on. Isn't that a fact? And perceptions in this part of the world, the Balkans, as you called it, matter; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And by your earlier answer, Izetbegovic showed his true colours because he did not follow the constitution. He did not follow the laws. He bypassed you and went for his fellow Muslim because he didn't trust a Croat, and that's how it was perceived by the Croats, wasn't it? And that's why you were being criticised as well by all members in your own party; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must understand the situation. Who could have commanded all that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Answer the question. Whether he was more competent than you, that's a different issue. I'm talking about perceptions. You were voted by the Croatian people to represent them at the Presidency, sir. And this was televised. This was live. And Izetbegovic showed every Croat in Bosnia-Herzegovina that you didn't matter and that he reached out and went for someone else. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We're back to argument and speeches, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We are back to arguments and speeches. The witness has given his answer, it's not the answer Mr. Karnavas wants, Mr. Karnavas just wants to argue with the witness, and I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He hasn't answered the question, Your Honour. That's the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because this came up, did it not, sir, within party politics, that you had been bypassed visibly, for the whole world to see, at a most critical point of time when -- at a most critical point of time when Bosnia-Herzegovina was being attacked.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent. But I cannot have a fight with Izetbegovic over that because of my pride.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I -- I understand you, sir. As long as we made the point for the record, and I think we have, we can move on. Now, on that particular day --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sorry, Your Honour, no. We object to that. What Mr. Karnavas says is not evidence. He says he's made the point. There is no point to be made by Mr. Karnavas's question. A question gives no information to the Court whatsoever. It is a question, it is not evidence. And unless the witness is given a chance, if he needs to, to make a full answer to that, then there is no evidence and there is no point to be made. Mr. Karnavas's question is not evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll break it down Your Honour. I'll go step-by-step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Karnavas. Stop there for a moment. The Judges are going to interpret what both sides have said. Place your trust in the Bench. Now, the question that the witness has been asked, in this situation where Mr. Izetbegovic was taken into custody by the Serbs and normally you should have replaced him, not Mr. Ganic, now, the question that the Defence is asking you - and this corresponds to the defence's strategy - since you were not designated, now, with respect to your Croat compatriots, did you not appear to be somebody who had been slighted by Mr. Izetbegovic and could your fellow Croats doubt you in any way because of that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They could not doubt me because I was in Sarajevo throughout. That's the first point. Secondly, that was an improper gesture on Izetbegovic's part, a sleight of hand, but that didn't mean that I had to enter into a fight with Izetbegovic. I just took note of that in my own head. But the general situation was such that sometimes you have to pass over something and tolerate something. I didn't see this as an attack on my pride or any particular slight, and it never entered my head that I could clash with the Muslims because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Kljuic, let's forget your feelings for the moment, what you felt at the time. Did the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, legally elected, was it functioning? Did it function pursuant to the rules, regulations, and principles? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until that point, yes, it did, but once they threw me out, it wouldn't have functioned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, in any country, democratic country, constitutionally based, can we consider this kind of gesture where the president of the Presidency violates the rules and is replaced and gives authorisation as if the state were his property, gives authority to somebody else by skipping you over, is that considered a -- an attack, a state coup?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not a state coup, but it was improper.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now in democratic states, is this considered to be a coup d'etat, regardless of what you may think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. A coup d'etat is when the army replaces democratically elected governments.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kljuic, a state coup can be effected through an army, but it can also be a violation of the constitution. Was the constitution essentially violated here, the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was a violation of the constitution and of standard practice as well, and customs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you'll make up -- we'll make up for the time used by Mr. Praljak when he intervened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we can always use intervention from a general to get to the heart of the matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just to touch up on the last question, that constitutional violation was also viewed by everyone. It wasn't something that was kept secret. This was played on national television. Right? Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was, but in the constitution it doesn't say -- it isn't written. This isn't written strictly speaking. That was practice and that was protocol, but much more important than that was the general impression it left on me, for example, when he promoted Ganic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the general impression that it left on you with respect to those who had voted you in is that the Croats are not being represented or are being bypassed by Izetbegovic. That's the essence of the questioning here. That on national television the Croats saw that Izetbegovic doesn't really care about the constitution, and in time of crisis he's not going to reach out to the next person because he's a Croat but, rather, he'll reach out to a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm going to object again. I said I would object all afternoon and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He can object all he wants, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I will. These are just arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, ask your question so that the witness can answer, without making speeches yourself. Everybody understood the legal problem and constitutional issues, so ask him. Or I'll ask him. You have been following the debate, Witness. Now, from the aspects of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was there a legal obligation on the part of Mr. Izetbegovic to nominate you in his place rather than Mr. Ganic? Was this a written rule or a custom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was customary and protocol to do so. Take the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for instance, and then you'll see that, unfortunately, that is not the case. However, much more than that act was a political message that was promoted here. So don't ask us to enter into a clash with the Muslims at a point in time when the Serb units were bombing all the territory populated by other people including the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is the procedure, sir -- is this in the rules of procedure as to who's next in line?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which? What?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, after Izetbegovic -- after -- hold on. After Izetbegovic, were you not next in line and was that not in the rules of procedure as to who would be next in line?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that that was the established practice during Communist times, and it was continued and is implemented today, too, but it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- doesn't say anywhere specifically -- what rules of procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just be of assistance and use the real word. I don't think the witness understands. The rules of procedure, known as "poslovnik."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the rules of proceedure or "poslovnik" is not a constitutional category. All right. If you say that that is how it was, I was the one who was slighted, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, on the 4th -- we'll go back. On the 3rd of May and the 4th of May, Siroki Brijeg was shelled. Do you recall that event?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On the 6th of May, 2.000 -- 200 -- 230.000 refugees from BiH are in Croatia, or go to Croatia. I believe are in Croatia at that point in time. 230.000; is that about right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need for you to mention figures. As armed actions were undertaken, people left certain regions, and the only place that they fled to was to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On the 10th of May, Mostar was heavily damaged and cut off from the rest of the world, more or less; right? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those are -- that is the information that we received every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we had testimony here in this court as well that on the 13th of May, 1992, habitants from the east side of Mostar were escaping to the west side of Mostar under some rather treacherous conditions. Does at that ring a bell, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were attacked by the JNA. They're Serbo-Chetnik volunteers and therefore they had to flee to the west where the majority population was Croatian and you had the units of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. The one that they had armed themselves and prepared themselves for war because they saw what was about to happen. We discussed this earlier today. Now on the 17th [Realtime transcript read in error "3rd"] of May it is recorded that 28.000 shells hit Mostar. Does that sound about right to you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it sounds -- it means a lot to me, yes. It sounds about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sounds about right. All right. On the 19th of May, HDZ and --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: H -- When you say "a lot," are you disputing the figure or is this something --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not disputing figures. I lived in a city where there were shells every day, lots of them, and if I were to tell you that on the 14th of May in Sarajevo, for example, there were so many shells that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We can move on, point made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, just a correction. My understanding is that the date was not the 3rd of May but it was the 17th of May, I'm told. There may have been a transcript error.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 17th of May. 17th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, on 19 May, 1992, it's my understanding that HDZ and SDA of Mostar signed an agreement about joint fighting against the Serbs on BiH territory. And the Muslims in Mostar issued calls for all their fighters to join the HVO. Were you aware of that, sir? Does that sound about right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I'm not quite sure whether that local agreement applied to the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but certainly it had pretensions of being for the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I believe we heard some testimony, but we'll hear some more, that on the 23rd of May, 1992, Mostar was more or less in flames. The right castle of the old bridge was damaged by shells and the city hall was as well. Does that sound about right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, while Mr. Karnavas has stopped, I just want to note for the record I'm a little disturbed about the nature of this questioning and answering. I don't know if Mr. Karnavas takes it that these things have been established just because the witness says something sounds about right, or probably. I'm just concerned this way of presentation is as if these facts are conclusively established, and for the record, I note my concern about this way of establishing facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the court deals with objections, not concerns, but if he has a concern, earlier I noted that during the course of the proceedings we will be proving up these dates and that we're not going to rely simply on the gentleman's memory, but this is merely to show the gap of the events that happened from the first time to now, and so I take the concern to heart and I'm sure I'm not telling the Prosecutor something that he doesn't know or should know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, on the 14th of June, 1992, HVO liberated the east side of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please let me just tell you this. You have a piece of paper in front of you -- Just wait. Let me tell you. I'm not your slave here. I lived through all that. I'm a victim of all that. I experienced it all, and what I want to say is this: There was shelling every day. You have before you a piece of paper and you say 3, 5, 4, 7. There was shelling every day. I don't have a document in front of me, I don't have an aide-memoire or anything like that, I assume that what you're saying is correct, but we're not on a footing of equality and you're asking me now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir, but the question was not about the shelling of Sarajevo. You were in Sarajevo but not in Mostar, and the Defence is asking you now whether on the 23rd of May Mostar was in flames. So you either saw it on television or not. So say yes or no. You were not there. And then they said the 19th of June the HVO liberated Mostar. Do you know this? Yes or no. If you do, say yes, if not, no, I don't know. So you're not being asked about Sarajevo. For the moment, for the time being, the questions refer to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the shelling of Mostar is concerned, it was daily shelling. As for the liberation of Mostar, that was one of the happiest, joyous moments that we experienced, all citizens in favour of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for that. Now, we'll go to the 20th of June, 1992. That's when we have the decision on pronouncement of state of war. That would have been at the state level, no? So you would have been a part of it, or aware of it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So -- so it takes at least the -- the state to react several months and finally declare a pronouncement of state war after we -- we've heard that Mostar has been in flame, you know, and heavily damaged. Other parts of the country are -- have been shelled, like Siroki Brijeg. The president has been detained and ransomed. You bypassed in the meantime, and so on and so forth. So finally on the 20th of June, the government, or the -- I should say the state, the Presidency, finally pronounces a state of war. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, motion to strike. I make a motion to strike the statement -- the speech by Mr. Karnavas from the record. We don't seem to be making any other communication. He just continues doing it, and I ask that the question be stricken from the record and then Mr. Karnavas put a correct question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is the Prosecution doubting the events that we just covered? I mean, he's been in the case for several years. These are all facts, they're going to be proved in this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's a question of proper procedure, Your Honour. It's a question of proper procedure. Pure and simple. This is not the way that you put questions to a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have one last question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you gave us a series of dates and then raised questions and asked the witness about everything that had taken place over the space of several months. Now, you should now come to a question which is a conclusion. So what is the concluding question that you're going to ask the witness? A question with a conclusion. We're going to listen and record what we're told. Perhaps your dates have some logic, perhaps they don't. So ask your final question and we'll see what happens, what the answer is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. -- I was attempting to do that. I did it inartfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You indicated to us that Bosnia-Herzegovina was declared and acknowledged to be independent as of April, April 6th, 1992. You stated that and that's a fact, is it not, sir?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you omitted to say that on the 22nd it became a member of the United Nations, the 22nd of May, which was to change defence strategy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Be that as it may. And here we are in June 20th, 1992, when a decision is pronounced on the state of war; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And between those two periods we covered all of these events which you acknowledged to either knowing -- personally knowing or knowing of; the various shellings of Mostar, Siroki Brijeg, and other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then it's not -- and then on 3 July, 1992, that brings us to the revision of the decision. Now, one last question. At this point in time, in light of the events, in light, as you have testified here today, that Sarajevo was under siege, that the state institutions, some of them, were not functioning, at least not to the extent that they should, some were not providing the services that they could, Sarajevo was cut off from the rest of the country and the rest of the country was cut off from Sarajevo. In light of all these circumstances, is it your belief that the state could still provide the necessary assurances to the people in the country and the services that it needed to provide, or was it necessary for folks outside of Sarajevo to self-manage themselves as they had been taught under this 50-year policy, this military Doctrine of All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the question has been properly formulated. Will you answer the question now, which is obviously important in view of all the questions leading up to this one final question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The official powers and authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina could not ensure the protection of all citizens. However, when we became members of the United Nations, the United Nations Charter was great encouragement for us, because it says there that if a Member State is attacked, then the international community is duty-bound to defend that State. The second point is this: We were not able to declare a state of war earlier until we had gathered up our defence potentials, because had we declared a state of war, let's say in April, then we gave the Yugoslav People's Army and the Chetnik volunteer units the right to shoot at us legally, because for as long as we did not declare a state of war, everything was irregular, and we didn't have the power to stand up to them, because you must realise that throughout the month of May there was the fight to pull out people from the barracks in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I happened to take part in those negotiations. The Serbs and the JNA always asked the Serb soldiers to be able to leave the barracks with dignity. We let them leave, but we took their weapons away. I don't want to tell you and go into detail what they did to those weapons to make them -- to put them out of order, but we -- that's what we did. We didn't have the necessary defence potential to be able to stand up to the other side, and that is why we procrastinated with this declaration of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, but you don't quite answer the question, because the question was a very specific question. Was this situation to lead to their own -- to the protection of some people who were to find the way in which to protect themselves? Public services were not working. Sarajevo was under siege. The Serbs were everywhere, and there was shelling. Does this not mean that the Croats had to take certain steps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not only the Croats but all citizens who were able to organise themselves, and it was quite normal to expect that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you answer the question by saying all citizens had to get organised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... been a good thing had everybody organised themselves, but you must differentiate between citizens firing at us and citizens defending themselves. Those who were firing were well organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, we are reaching the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, we have, and I don't want to keep the -- the translators any longer. I need about another hour, hour and 15 minutes with the gentleman. I have four chapters. I suspect that we can deal with this when we see the gentleman again. They are critical, but they're not -- they shouldn't take too long. And I will try to, in the meantime, be -- to streamline my questioning, but as you could see, it takes a while to get to the point, but I think we've covered the major difficult issues, and I'll try to readjust my questioning so that perhaps Mr. Scott will not have the concerns that he had today, and I'll take on board his observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think if you streamline your questions you should also discuss this with the other Defence counsel, because perhaps some issues were to -- were going to be raised by some other Defence counsel. There's no point in repeating the same questions. So if they intended putting the question, you better check that out with them. So we have to now finish the hearing. Witness, you will have to be called back. During the month of August and September, are there days where you cannot come to the Tribunal or are you available at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't give you an answer to that now. When I go back home I shall have to consult my diary and see what commitments I have. You know that the pre-election campaign is coming up. I'm an advisor, an assistant, I'm not an active participant, but I will take part in it. And then, of course, there is the holidays. My wife is a physician. She -- her job is not as flexible. She has to take her annual holiday at a given period of time, but I'm sure we will be able to find a date that is suitable to all of us, and you could perhaps propose two or three dates and I will do my best to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott is on his feet. He certainly had a number of dates to suggest. What kind of dates were you going to suggest?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The calendar is full, actually, as it now stands, for August, for reasons -- I won't go into all the names in open session - it may or not be a problem - but the first available time would be the week of the 4th of -- the week of the 4th of September, Your Honour. That would be the first date, and then I suppose it could be the following week as well. The 4th -- the week of the 4th, the week of the 11th. Obviously the Prosecution needs to know as soon as possible as well so we can schedule other witnesses around that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And Mr. President, I would ask that we have a full day. So if we could have, like, four sessions, just to be on the safe side. So -- it's a long trip. So we can -- it doesn't matter if it's three hours or five hours, I understand it's the same inconvenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we would have to start on a Monday. In an ideal situation, I think if we start on a Monday -- I think the 4th is a Monday, and I think the 11th is a Monday. Are you unable to come on the 4th of September or the 11th of September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- I can't on the 4th, not at all. As for the 11th, I will see, or I'll propose a different date; the 18th, perhaps, or the 25th, and I will let your office know in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the problem is we have to work out our schedule beforehand. This is rather difficult sometimes, so we have to -- if you tell us that you can come on the 4th, fine. If you tell us on the 11th, fine. But you have just said that you cannot come on the 4th. So let's assume you can come on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. I would suggest after the 1st of October, if possible, because then I will be free.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. The office in Sarajevo will tell you when to come back. I would like to thank you. I wish you a safe journey home. And we shall all reconvene next week on Monday at a quarter past 2.00. I'd like to thank you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 3rd day of July, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.43 p.m.,
